speechtext: It is desirable to have a surplus in the Post Office Department as well as any other department, but not by means of overpaying or overworking the officials. I do not pretend to know anything of the facts in controversy betw'een the hon. gentleman and my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk), but I could not very well gather from the Postmaster General whether he considers that these men should not be paid for over work or that no overwork is imposed on them. He was not very clear on that point. In the railway service I understand that a system is adopted under which a certain number of miles is regarded as a day's work of an engineer or conductor or other trainman, and any additional number of miles is paid for extra. If the problem which has been brought to our attention by my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier could not be solved in any other way, perhaps it could be dealt with on some such system as that. If I am not interfering in the discussion which my hon. friend has raised, I would like to draw attention to the presentment of the grand jury of the county of Halifax, made in the term of last March. It is reported in the press as follows :

In the case of O'Connell, charged with stealing from the Postmaster General, the grand jury yesterday made the following presentment :-
As a result of investigations in the case of the King vs. O'Connell, charged with stealing registered packages from the bag of a letter-carrier, and from personal observations, the grand jury beg to call attention to the urgent need of largely increased facilities for the more prompt delivery of, and greater protection to. letters and other mail matter for the people of Halifax.
From the facts within the knowledge of the grand jury, it appears that though the amount of mail matter received at the Halifax post office has increased fivefold within a period of twenty-five or thirty years, the staff of letter-carriers, though increased from five to twenty-three, is not enough for the needs of the service now demanded ; while it is a very suggestive fact that the inside staff has actually decreased in number during that period.
The inevitable result follows, viz., that the men are not only overworked and the people do not obtain that prompt delivery of the mails enjoyed by much smaller cities all over the Dominion, hut, because of insufficient staff, ordinary letters as well as registered Sir WILLIAM MULOCK.
matter are not accorded that protection from robbery that the public expect and demand.
The grand jury beg to recommend that, in order to insure the ample protection to all mail matter, and for more prompt delivery to the people of Halifax, the Post Office Department be urged to provide additional help both for the inside and outside service ; and that the postmaster should take the necessary steps to see that no carrier be permitted to leave the office with a heavier load and larger bundles than he can handle with despatch and safety from loss, as is now frequently the case.
If this statement is in accord with the facts, it discloses a somewhat serious condition of affairs. Men are described as overworked and the public is not receiving that accommodation from the public service to which it is entitled. No doubt this presentment has been brought to the attention of the Postmaster General. Has he made any investigation into its allegations and with what result ? The body which has made these presentments is an important one, selected from the most influential citizens of the city and county of Halifax, and I am sure they would not make statements without having the proofs of what they allege.

This is the first I have heard of the presentment in question, but my deputy informs me that the chief city superintendent of post offices, Mr. Ross, visited Halifax a short time ago on his usual round, and reported the staff as up to par. There is no insufficiency in it. As to the general presentation itself, it has been referred to Mr. Ross for investigation, and he will investigate as soon as possible. It is very easy for people in the best of faith to be carried away with the idea that the remedy for any evil or misfortune is an increase in the staff. It is a chronic idea throughout the whole public service that if anything is wrong, the best way to right it is to engage additional hands. I do not want to reflect on the service, but whoever has charge of the transaction of business in any walk of life knows that an increase in the staff is always very popular among the employees. There is no intention of skimping the service anywhere, but I believe you could not do any greater injury to the service itself than to have it overmanned. The statement that the employees are overworked is without foundation. Of course there are emergency occasions in every post office when the clerks must work overtime, but that is inseparable from the duties of the office and is part of their engagement. But as to that being the normal condition, such a statement is altogether unfounded, and those who made it have been misled.

I shall not enter into any controversy on that point. The report of Mr. Ross seems singularly inconsistent with the statement of these gentlemen who

had this matter investigated before them under oath. I have discharged my duty by bringing the matter to the attention of the Postmaster General. I should be inclined to think that men such as those of whom, to my own knowledge, the grand jury of Halifax, is composed, would not make a statement of that kind without very good foundation for it; and until I was more sure of the thoroughness of Mr. Ross's investigation, 1 would not be prepared to accept his statement rather than that which has been made by the grand jury.
I wish to bring to the attention of the Postmaster General another matter as to which I have had some communication through the public press and otherwise-the salaries of the second-class clerks in the outside service in the post office at Halifax. I understand that some representation has been made to the Postmaster General on that point, and that those interested have put forward cogent reasons why their salaries should be taken into consideration, especially, I believe, some who have been in the service a long time and who have not received the consideration which has been extended to others of more recent appointment. I would like to ask the Postmaster General whether their representations have been taken into consideration, and whether it is likely that any change for the better will be made in their case, especially those of long service in the department ?

If the hon. gentleman (Mr. R. L. Borden) wishes to ask whether it is the intention of the government to deal with the second-class clerks of the outside service as a class, I would say that it is not in contemplation at the present time, to pass legislation altering their status. As to promotions or increases, these are matters relating to individuals. It is our effort to promote deserving men, and we are constantly ascertaining those deserving of such recognition, for nothing gives me greater pleasure, in connection with my work, than to recognize the merit of those who are deserving. It may be possible- but I doubt it very much-that there are one or more persons in the Halifax post office who are not being properly remunerated for their services. Length of service, in a sense, is a reason for promotion, but it is only one ground for such recognition. It is a consideration, and an important one; nevertheless the requirements of the service, the duties performed and the remuneration actually received, are all elements to be considered in each individual case. Mr. Ross makes it his business to consult with the city postmasters from time to time to see whether merit is being duly rewarded and whether there are any deserving men being underpaid. If, by any chance, there is an oversight, it is purely accidental, because, as I stated before it is a source of special pleasure to me, at all times, to recognize merit.

I understand that what I am referring to relates both to a class and to individuals as well. I understand that the second-class clerks in the Halifax post office represent that the cost of living is greatly increased, that their opportunities of promotion to first-class rank are very small, and they are desirous, as I understand it that they be permitted to obtain a maximum salary of $1,500. I also alluded to others who might be entitled, without change in the law, to higher salaries than those which they enjoy at present and who consider themselves as much entitled to certain increases of salary as men of more recent appointment who have been accorded that increase. It is on behalf of the class, and on behalf of the individuals to whom I refer that I am making this representation. I hope the Postmaster General will not regard the matter as finally closed but will take the case of these men into consideration. It is possible, as he says, that some of these men may have been accidently overlooked. Of course, it is not the slightest consolation to them that they have been overlooked by accident
I did not refer to the matter in that sense.

I know that. But, if these gentlemen had been overlooked by accident, it is just as unfortunate for them as if they had been overlooked by design. Therefore, there may be some reason for further consideration of the matter, and I hope that consideration will be given.

I suppose the hon. gentleman is aware that the salary of a second-class clerk in the city post office of Halifax goes to $1,200, the minimum being $900. My hon. friend (Mr. R. L. Borden) will know better than I what is the average salary paid to persons in Halifax performing services not calling for greater ability or more arduous labour than is required of a second-class clerk. Some little proportion must be maintained between the two things. At the same time, my view is that, in this age, the government should be, more or less, a model employer, and, where there is any doubt should lean in the direction of higher salaries. I endeavour to carry out that policy and to see to it that the staff are paid not less, but at least a shade more than is paid for similar services in private walks of life. I may say that it is the practice of the department now to overhaul the whole staff of the outside service yearly with a view to considering cases of promotion. The case of each individual is investigated. That examination has been going on throughout the whole of Canada for some little time.

Of one thing you may be pretty sure and that is that within the last eight or ten years the cost of liv-i ing has increased very considerably, as, also

has the general scale of salaries paid in the city of Halifax, I think that corporations and other employers of labour have been obliged to put their scale of salaries considerably higher than that which prevailed eight or ten years ago ; and it is largely on. this ground that these men make their application. Further, I think, the applicants represent that the clerks of the second class of the inside service have a maximum salary of $1,500. I do not know whether that is correct or not.
That is correct.

They represent that those in the outside service should be placed on the same basis, because their expenses are equally great, and they suffer from the increased cost of living and they see no reason why, with the long service they have rendered, they should not he entitled to a maximum salary equal to that enjoyed by those in the inside service.

I wish to remind the Postmaster General that some time ago I made a recommendation to the effect that there are several officers in Halifax post office, who through their length of service and efficiency might well be advanced from junior clerkships to a higher grade. I would beg to again call his attention to that. There has been no surplus of clerks there and recently the work of the Post Office Department has been increased by the very large amount of literature which has been sent there for distribution to the various portions of the county of Halifax.

Some few
weeks ago when my hon. friend (Mr. Wm. Roche) brought this matter to my notice it was referred to Mr. Ross, the inspector, for investigation, and there are now in the department reports from Mr. Ross upon the subject which my deputy is now going through.

I wish to call the attention of the Postmaster General to the necessity of repairs in the Galt post office. There is but one entrance to the building and when the mails are being distributed there is great crowding and in cold weather the doors are kept open by the crowd, so that it is very uncomfortable. If there was another door people could pass out that way, and avoid crushing. There should also be a private office for the postmaster himself and there is an insufficient number of post office boxes. These matters should be attended to at once, and improvements similar to those in the Berlin post office should be made there.

Communications were received some time ago upon this subject, the Galt post office was visited by the inspector and he made a recommendation which has been approved of by the Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
Post Office Department and has been forwarded to the Public Works Department, so that I have very good reason to believe that the improvements suggested will be carried out.
Then I suppose there will be in the supplementary estimates an amount for the necessary changes, so that the work will be done before the cold weather comes on.

I wish the Minister of Public Works was here so that he would feel the benefit of my hon. friend's appeal, but I shall call his attention to it again although as I say the Post Office Department has already communicated to the Public Works Department the necessity for the alterations referred to.

I would like to again mention to the Postmaster General what I mentioned to him last year, that is that very serious complaints come to me every now and again with regard to the mail service at Vankleek Hill. I suppose that these complaints also come to the Postmaster General and that he has taken them into consideration. Is there to be any amelioration of the situation described in very glowing terms in some of these communications which I have received ?
I do not like to speak from memory lest my memory be incorrect, but if my hon. friend will let me have the memorandum I shall inquire into this matter.

I would also like to call attention to the raising of the rates of book postage from 4 to 8 cents per pound. Would the Postmaster General be good enough to inform me as to whether that is a recent change or not ?
The rates of book postage in Canada have been brought into harmony with those in the United States and other countries within the postage union, that is, one cent for two ounces.
What was the rate before ?
One cent for four ounces.
The rate has been doubled by the hon. gentleman ?
The present rate is one cent for two ounces, which is the postal union rate.
And the rate before was one cent for four ounces ?
That is what it was.
How much additional revenue does my hon. friend hope to get by that increase ?
Practically nothing, very little I presume.
Can the minister not inform me within 85,000 or $10,000 what increase he expects in the revenue of the department ?
I have no way of forming an accurate estimate.
What is the idea in increasing the rate if the hon. gentleman has no idea of an increased revenue ?
We were the only country which had the low rate.
How much additional revenue does the minister hope to get ?

While it is quite impossible to give figures it is quite possible to show that the experience of other countries is of some assistance to us. We were the only country in the wide world carrying books at such a rate as one cent' for four ounces and we have only fallen into line with the rest of the world by making the rate one cent for two ounces.

The hon. gentleman has been claiming that we were leading the way in other respects but we are not leading the way in this very important respect. Why is it that we are receding ? Why is it that we are retrograding in this regard by adopting a system which must result in discouraging the circulation of good literature. Good books ought to be distributed amongst the people of the country, and why should you tax the people double the amount which they were formerly taxed for the transmission of books ? Is not that a somewhat serious consideration ? We have a very large country and a sparse population and it is desirable that the people should receive books as cheaply as possible. As we have been leading the way for so many years in the matter of book postage, why is it that we are retrograding, going back, and keeping the rate simply as the hon. Postmaster General says at what has prevailed in other countries ? I hardly regard the action of the Post Office* Department in this respect as being up to the high standard which the Postmaster General lias claimed for it in other regards.
The fact is that we have had to carry so much Tory dead-head literature through the mails that we must compensate ourselves in some way.
The hon. gentleman admitted that he sent out a great deal more from his side of the House than from the opposition side and so he had better give himself credit for that.
I did not admit it.

I do not think we should follow the example of the United States in this regard or in a great many
other ways. I think that we should progress rather than go back. I had interviews with a number of gentlemen of different professions in Halifax before I left and they informed me that when they got books that were expensive and which belonged to the different professions with which they are connected they consider the postage a great burden. I think the Postmaster General has taken a step in this respect in the wrong direction.

At six o'clock the hon. member for Victoria, Nova Scotia (Mr. Ross) was expressing his regret that the hon. gentleman the Postmaster General had seen fit to double the postage rate on books sent through the mails, and we were trying to ascertain from the hon. gentleman what it was that prompted him to make the change. The only explanation was that he wanted to make the rate uniform with that which obtained in other countries in the Postal Union. We endeavoured to ascertain from the hon. gentleman how much lie hoped to increase the revenue of the Post Office Department h/ that change but we have not yet been able to get that information. I have heard of no general demand for an increased rate on books on the part of the public. There was no petition sent in asking that the rate be increased. It must have been increased for the purpose of implementing the revenue of the department. I would ask the hon. minister how much he hopes to increase the revenue b.\ doubling the rate.

I understand that the revenue from the book rate is comparatively trifling and t lie re fore no very serious addition to the revenue would be made. Something would be made but I understand that the old rate did not anything like pay the cost of the service.

Is there no estimate of the revenue from newspapers, letters, parcels and books ? There must be some estimate in the department of the probable revenue from these sources. Surely we might expect the hon. Postmaster General to be able to give us some information as to how much he hopes to increase the revenue by the increased rate on books which he has imposed.

I do not know whether the hon. gentleman stated that there was no estimate of the increased revenue derived from these various classes of mail matter, but if he did so he was in error. There are estimates as to the revenue from newspaper postage, but there are no data

5720 '

as to the revenue derived from other branches of the service. On reflection the hon. gentleman will see that it would be impossible to have definite data upon that subject. Take a post office like that of Toronto for instance", all classes of mail matter, letters, circulars, parcels and newspapers are rushed in at the last moment probably for the outgoing mail. The work of stamping sorting and despatching occupies the time until the close of the out-going mail and it would not be possible to keep tab on all the different classes of mail matter going through the office. I can conceive of no possibility of doing that.
There might be a large revenue for all the hon. gentleman knows by reason of the increased rate.

Any person who goes into a post office will see that the volume of books as compared with other classes of mail matter is comparatively trifling.
Mi*. CLANCY. But, including parcels with books on which the hon. gentleman has increased the postage it would have been a matter of very great interest to the country if the hon. Postmaster General could have come down and stated the increase that the revenue had by reason of increasing the postage on that class of mail matter such as books, pamphlets and parcels, the transmission of which, the hon. gentleman knows, has immensly increased throughout the country.
WThat has immensely increased ?

The business of the Post Office in handling that class of matter as the hon. Postmaster General's deputy will tell him has immensely increased. Having doubled the postage on that class of mail matter, he must expect to receive an immense addition to the revenue.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) speaks without information. The volume of parcel postal matter has not materially increased.

I want to say to the hon. the Postmaster General that if he is deriving his information from his deputy who is sitting beside him, it is at variance with such statements as one can put his hand upon and compile in one of the departments of the government. And I may tell the hon. gentleman that I will point that out later on to him.
Proceed.

I do not know whether you mean by book-post simply books, but the volume of business in matter that is partly printed and can be filled up in writing, such as deeds and agreements and docu-Slr WILLIAM MULOCK.
ments of that kind, has increased very much. I know from having to do with some work of that kind, that our postage has increased one-half or one-third since the change was made. The increased rate means quite an increased cost to loan companies, and insurance companies and institutions of that kind.

The law fixes the rate of postage on letters, and surely a person cannot take a blank form partly printed and fill up his ideas on that in writing, and have it regarded as a letter. 1 am not aware of any government that allows such an evasion of the law.
The question is not whether any one is trying to evade the law, but Whether the people pay more now than formerly.
Formerly it was impossible for postmasters to tell what was the proper rate.
It is so yet.
No.
So at least one postmaster has told me. V
My hon. friend has allowed himself to be deceived ; he is too readily loaded up against the government.
The friends of the government have told me so.

They do not tell us that. Postmasters complained formerly that the rates on different classes of mailable matter were intricate. If I had the statute here, I could show that it would take a Philadelphia lawyer to make out what was the proper rate to be charged on lithograph matter and printed matter, for example. Either the postmasters had to open the documents, or refer to the department at Ottawa, or take chances on collecting the proper postage, and often one person paid one rate- and another person paid a different rate on the same class of matter. It was most inconvenient, and therefore we put many of these things into one class, so that all persons would be treated equally. It was not done so much for the sake of revenue as to put the business on a proper basis.
It may be better now than it was before, but it is ambiguous yet. I have been called on to discuss the matter with more than one postmaster.
On what item ?

The Markdale postmaster, for instance.
iSir WILLIAM MULOCK. I asked, on what item ?

Take blank certificates done up in the ordinary tube, which are all

printed matter except the signature. What class would they be in ? I cannot tell the exact percentage of increase in the rates, hut nay experience is that the increase is at least one-third more than before.
It is merely a simplification.

Friendly benevolent organizations, in sending out their reports, have to pay just double the postage they did previously. Surely the minister cannot assert that he has no knowledge as to how much the revenue has been increased as a result of this change, which must have been made for the purpose of getting more revenue. "Would it be $150,000 or $200,000 ? Occasionally I see a statement issued as to the number of letters, postal cards and newspapers passing through the mails. Are these actually counted, or is there an estimate made ? If this can be done, I should think that the minister ought to be able to give us an idea as to how much he has increased the revenue by this additional tax. It is not a popular tax, and in view of the financial statement the minister has made. I rather astonished he did not take it off. The hon. gentleman says that those who complain are not friends of the government, hut I would point out that in this evening's Montreal ' Star ' there is a letter from a prominent Liberal, well known in the community, Mr. Norman Murray, a bookseller in Montreal, who draws attention to this very matter. Mr. Murray writes :
At the close of the last financial year the Post Office Department had a surplus of nearly $300,000, yet they raised the book postage from 4 cents to 8 cents a pound. Now I call myself a real Liberal, but I fail to see what the Liberalism of the party in power consists of.
I am sure the Postmaster General must know Mr. Murray as a political friend'. At all events, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries would probably know him very well.
Mr. PREtFONTAINE. I know him.

If there were a surplus to the credit of the Post Office Department, why should the postal rate on books be doubled ? It must have been done for the purpose of increasing the revenue, and the Postmaster General must have some idea as to the extent of the increase of revenue by this additional taxation. Are we to have no answer ?
I have explained to the hon. gentleman twice, and I am quite willing to repeat, if that be deemed necessary. The hon. gentleman asks whether there are statistics upon which to base an estimate

Not that ; I assumed, and I think fairly, that the object of doubling the rate on books was to increase the revenue.
and I asked the Postmaster General if he could not give some approximate idea at least as to how much he hoped to increase the revenue by the imposition of this additional tax. I do not ask the hon. gentleman to give me the exact amount, but approximately. Would it be $50,000 or $100,000 ?

The hon. gentleman is talking wildly. All governments have some regard to rates. The late government fixed one cent an ounce as the cost of carrying merchandise, regarding that rate as appropriate. That is still the rate. In fixing that rate, I suppose the government had some reference to the cost of transportation. Therefore half that rate does not seem unreasonable as the book rate. When the hon. gentleman asks for information as to the revenue derivable from book postage, I ask him to imagine himself in a post office when mail matter is coming in or going out, and see if he can form au intelligent idea of the amount of books compared with other mailable matter passing through the office. There are books, parcels, circulars, newspapers, letters and whatever else is mailable, all bundled oil perhaps at the last moment. All the staff can do is to sort the matter and put the various parcels in the respective bags to which they belong, and out goes the whole volume of mail matter. How would it be possible under these circumstances to have statistics, or to form any intelligent idea of the volume of the different classes of mail matter posted at a particular post office ? It is a practical impossibility. It is not done anywhere, and it could not be done unless we chose to suspend the proper despatching of the mails in order to keep account.
I understand from the minister that he does not know anything as to the probable increase of revenue from this form of taxation ?
It must be a comparative trifle.
I suppose it would not be more than $100,000 at any rate ?
The hon. gentleman knows full well that in suggesting $100,000 he is talking wildly.
Do not the country postmasters keep an account of the sale of postage stamps, postcards and money orders?

A postmaster in the country, who is paid by commission, is paid upon the revenue of his office and tlie number of special services he performs. He is paid a commission upon the postage stamps and postcards sold, the volume of the money order business, the postal note business, and the savings bank business if it is a savings bank branch. He is also

sometimes allowed something for night work, an allowance called a forwarding allowance, and an allowance for rent, fuel and light. These allowances are based upon the business done in the office. That is a very different thing from keeping the record of the different classes of mailable matter that go out.

Is there not a system in force of instructing the postmaster, say in a town office, for two weeks or a month to keep a strict account of all letters, postcards and other matter which pass out of the office, so that his salary may to a certain extent be based on the result ? [DOT]

About twice each year an enumeration, as it is called, is made in the different post offices, of the different classes of mail matter and the revenue derived therefrom. That system prevails only where the postmasters are paid by percentages. But even in those cases, there is nothing in the enumeration list to distinguish books from any other class of mail matter in which they are included. The enumeration divides the mailable matter into four classes-letters and post cards, newspapers, merchandise, and miscellaneous, which is a very large class, and which includes books.

As the bulk of the offices are not paid by salaries, but by fees, the amount of mail matter that comes in and goes out of each post office could easily be arrived at ; and it seems to me that books might be made a distinct class, like postcards and letters.

The hon. gentleman is in error in saying that nearly all the officers are on the percentage basis. Numerically he is right, but not so far as volume of business is concerned. I would say off-hand that quite one-third of the revenue is derived from offices where the staff is not paid by way of commissions.
The minister has stated that he could give the committee the amount of revenue derived from newspapers. Would he be good enough to give that ?
I gave that two days ago, in answer to a question. It is in ' Hansard.'

The hon. gentleman reduced the rate, I think, from one-half to one-quarter cent per pound. Could he state how this change affected the revenue ? Another change which the hon. gentleman made was to permit a person wishing to mail say one hundred printed pamphlets, to send them by making a cash payment instead of using postage stamps. How much revenue has he derived from that change? It is important to have ail this information Sir WILLIAM MULOCK.
in order that we may judge whether the changes made are in the interest of the country.

The hon. gentleman has asked what has been the effect of the revenue of the department of the reduction in the rate of postage on newspapers. I cannot give the figures, but the immediate effect was a very substantial loss of revenue. The newspapers however soon increased the volume of their output so as to bring the revenue up to almost where it was, and we are carrying a very much larger quantity of papers for the same money.
When was the rate of 1 cent a pound put on ?

I think about. 1898. One-quarter of a cent per pound was imposed on the 1st of July, 1898, and one-half a cent on the 1st of January, 1899. I understood my hon. friend to ask how much was paid by the publishers on mail matter in cash instead of in postage stamps. There is no account kept of that, but the reason of the change was this. The publishers found it inconvenient to affix a stamp, to each separate piece of mail matter ; and in order to save them trouble, the department provided for payment in bulk whenever the quantity of mail matter involved the payment of 825 or upwards. Instead of affixing a stamp to each separate piece, the publishers paid cash, and then the goods are marked ' Paid for in bulk.'
The hon. minister has said that the decrease in the rate of postage on newspapers has resulted iu an increase in circulation.
No, but I said there has been an increase in the quantity of newspapers sent through the mails.

I understood him to say that when his governpient made the postage one-half cent per pound on newspapers and afterwards reduced that to one-quarter of a cent, the immediate effect was a decrease in the revenue but shortly afterwards the revenue came up to its original amount. Therefore the effect of the increase in postage was an increase in the quantity of newspapers sent through the mails.
A larger weight, not a larger number.

My hon. friend says that the number of newspapers was not larger, but that the public got larger newspapers for the same money and therefore got the benefit. Would not the same effect follow a reduction in the postage on books ? My hon. friend has doubled the cost of sending books through the mails, and it is fair to assume that caused a decrease in the number of books going through and therefore caused great disadvantage to the public. He

claims a great deal of credit for his management of the department, and I suppose that some considerable portion of the credit he claims is Jue him, but it would be only fair to say that the change in book postage was not in the interests of the public but was rather for the purpose of increasing the revenue.

Whatever may be said about the effect of the postage on newspapers, I think there is one thing on which we can all agree, and that is that this country is not suffering from a dearth of newspapers. As to the rate of postage on books, when the hon. gentleman tries to draw a comparison between books and newspapers, I would say that the postal service is as full of anomalies in the matter of rates as is the railway service. The rates charged on one class of matter are not any guide to what might be the rates proper to charge on another class.
Why does not the hon. gentleman straighten out the anomalies ?
I must leave something for successors. Some day the hon. gentleman expects to be in my place, and I want to leave him something to do.

The tax upon the public in the matter of postage on newspapers amounted last year to $129,417 and for the ten months to the 30th of April this year to $100,071. That is the result of the decrease in the postal rate. If there is no perceptible increase as the result of doubling the postage on books, why not do away with the increased postage ?
Wrould it not be better to begin by making letters free and let everybody have the benefit ?
If you would reduce the tax on drop letters in cities from two to one cent, you would be conferring a great benefit on the public.
My hon. friend's colleague wants it reduced to one-half a cent.

You are doubling the rate on books and thus making it more difficult to disseminate information through the country. If you would reduce the drop letter rate from two cents to one cent, that reduction would be very much appreciated. There are, as the hon. gentleman admits, anomalies in the postal rates. The hon. gentleman will send out a circular, which weighs as much as four letters, and that *will be distributed by the same letter-carrier for a cent whereas a thin letter is charged two cents. At the same time a postal card is delivered at one cent. It is hardly worth while to continue the government tax on books.

Before taking off the postage on books, if we are going to
have free mail matter, why not begin with having free letters. If my hon. friend is in favour of free letters, let him say so. His colleague from Halton last night argued in favour of a reduction of the letter rate in cities from two cents per drop letter to one-' half cent.
I argued no such thing. I will explain later on what I did mean.
My hon. friend explained that the rate on drop letters in cities was excessive. Instead of two cents it should be one-half cent.

I beg the hon. minister's pardon. He was boasting about the large amount in postage he had saved to the people, and I simply remarked that in the cities he had saved nothing because the postage was two cents to-day as before.
I made no complaint and did not ask him either to increase or decrease the rate. All I did was simply state the fact that the hon. gentleman had neither increased nor decreased the postage rate in cities.

My hon. friend has quite forgotten what he told us. He used the term half-cent rate, and I took exception then, as I do now, to any such reduction. I took exception to his demand that the drop-letter rate in the cities should be reduced below two cents either to J cent or anything else and I took issue with the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) on the same proposition. If the hon. member (Mr. Henderson) will refer to ' Hansard ' he will see what he said. The hon. gentleman asks that we reduce the drop-letter rate from 2 cents to 1 cent. I said then as I say now that, inasmuch as the inhabitants of cities have their mail matter brought to them in their houses or offices, it is reasonable that they should pay more on some classes of mail matter than is paid by persons living at points not served by free carrier delivery. People in towns where there is no free delivery must go to the post office for their mail matter. And the government of hon. gentlemen opposite -not this government-decided that, in order to equalize matters, a higher rate should be paid on drop-letters in localities enjoying the letter carrier system than in others. I think that has been the policy of this country even since the free letter carrier system was established, 1 adhere to that policy. It is one of the few legacies of the late administration which commend themselves to the fair-mindedness of the people. I object to giving to the city advantages not enjoyed by the rural population, and at the same time giving them equally low rates. If cities are to have free delivery they ought to contribute something for the extra advantage they enjoy over their less fortunate fellow citizens in outlying points. And so I say the country will

not support the demand of the hon. member for Halton and the hon. member for West Toronto in this regard. Let the hon. gentleman go to his own constituency and tell the people of Oakville or Bronte that he suggested that the drop-letter rate in Toronto should be cut down from 2 cents to $ cent while the drop-letter rate in Oakville, Bronte and Milton should remain at 1 cent. I would like to know whether he will have the endorsement of the electors of the county of Halton in that ? I cannot believe that, on mature consideration, he will adhere to that view. I can understand the hon. member for West Toronto advocating it. It is quite in harmony with the interests of his own people, Probably it is his duty to present all phases of the question, that it may be argued and debated and reasons given for making the change or withholding it. I can understand that hon. gentleman advocating this change, as it is his duty to do in the interest of his constituents. But I cannot understand a gentleman representing a rural constituency advocating it. However, my view is that the cities which get the advantage of free delivery should pay something for the privileges they enjoy over less favoured parts of the country.

I am afraid the Postmaster General (Sir William Mulock) has wasted a good deal of wind on the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) and has worried himself unnecessarily as to the views his constituents in Oakville, Milton or Bronte may have as to what he said with reference to drop-letters in the city of Toronto or elsewhere. To be brief, I will read from ' Hansard ' what I did say. It fully corroborates the statement I made a moment ago-that I made no complaints about the Postmaster General not having reduced postage in the city of Toronto where there was free delivery. I did not ask him to do that ; I did not suggest that he should do it ; in fact I would not say that I would approve of his doing it. I was discussing the question of the redaction of postage. The hon. gentleman (Sir William Mulock) had boasted that he had done so much for the people and had reduced the postage by one-third. I simply pointed out that he had only reduced the postage in certain instances, not in all, and consequently the reduction did not amount to one-third. The statement I made with reference to the two-cent rate was as follows, as the hon. gentleman will And by referring to page 5822 of ' Hansard
What about the people In the cities who are paying a two cent rate on drop letters just the same as they have been paying previously ? How can the hon. gentleman come here and say that he has reduced the postage by one third ?
That is not all the hon. gentleman (Mr. Henderson) said.

That is all I said with reference to the postage in cities. Now sir WILLIAM MULOCK.
I will tell the hon. gentleman that I did suggest, and I will suggest again-and I think it is a very proper thing-that, in rural sections where there is no postal delivery it would be a very proper thing to reduce the postage on drop letters to i cent. I think that would be a very fair proposition. The government would not lose very much by it and it would be of material advantage to a great many people in the country. The hon. gentleman may know-because he is a business man-that merchants in the country towns and villages are taking advantage of the post office a great deal more than in former years for the purpose of advertising their wares. Instead of advertising so much in the newspapers, they draft a circular and send it to their customers or to the constituencies among which they do business. Possibly they do this three or four times a year. These letters are mostly drop-letters-letters addressed to persons at the post office at which the letters are posted. That is the kind of letter I referred to when I suggested that the postage might be reduced to i cent. I think that would only be in keeping with the privileges granted elsewhere. Why should I or any business man in my town put a one-cent stamp on a letter and drop it in the Acton post office to be delivered in that same post office without any expense to the government of carrying it through the mail ; when, for two cents, I can send a letter from Acton to Hong Kong? I do not think that that is reasonable, and1 I believe that the suggestion I make is only a fair one and one that is quite in harmony with the hon. gentleman's postal tariff. I trust the hon. gentleman now understands me fully, and that the severe strictures he made upon the argument he attributed to me that the rate on drop-letters where there is free delivery should be reduced to one-half cent will be withdrawn as being based upon a misapprehension. I am quite sure that it was a mere slip of the memory and that it was not done with the intention of arousing unnecessarily the indignation of my constituents in Oakville, Bronte and Milton. I remember that he was out there on one or two occasions and talked very largely about the deficit the Conservative party had-according to his statement-of $750,000 in the last year they were in power. The hon. gentleman paraded that deficit with all the volume of voice he was capable of spreading over the riding. But it all had no effect. The friend whom he took out from Toronto to supplant me returned shorn of his laurels. I fancy that the attack which he is going to make upon me in Oakville and Bronte and Milton on the matter of the unfairness that I suggest with reference to the postal rates as between these towns and Toronto will have just about the same effect and I hope the hon. gentleman when the time comes will pay us another visit .and give us another opportunity of seeing how effectual his arguments are

with the intelligent people of the county- X am speaking of the reasonable people of the county.

I am sorry that I riled the kon. gentleman in suggesting very respectfully-as I always address the hon. gentleman-that as he had doubled the tax on the people by the increase in the rate on books, he might take into consideration the advisability of giving them some relief in the matter of drop-letter rates. It is a fact that large firms in the city of Toronto, and X presume in Montreal, Ottawa and other large centres, deliver their letters themselves by messenger at a less cost than by the post and probably more speedily. For that reason I think the matter is one which should have the attention of the hon. gentleman, especially when he distributes circulars inclosed in envelopes weighing more thain ordinary letters and postal cards for a cent. If my memory serves me, he did not always speak out as vigorously against the proposition to reduce the drop-letter rate as he has done to-night. When a deputation waited on him in Toronto I think he held out the hope that something might be done, and I am sure they will be grieved and pained to hear his vigorous denial tonight at the mere suggestion to reduce the drop-letter rate. Might I ask if lie has any idea of the revenue derived in Toronto from drop-letters ?

It is very un fortunate that it is impossible to address a remark to the hon. member for West Toronto {Mr. Clarke) without his at once assuming that some terrible attack has been made upon him. It is all right for the hon. gentleman to present an argument, or what is advanced as an argument, but when a reply is made to it, then the hon. gentleman is personally attacked. I was commending the hon. gentleman for the attention he was giving to the interests of his constituents, and was in fact pointing out to him that in his absence he had found an advocate in the person of the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson), but my hon. friend is ungrateful to him. He says I did not always speak the same voice as to-night. I have never otherwise expressed myself than as I have done to-night It is true that a deputation from Toronto waited upon me two or three years ago and pressed this subject upon me. I held out no inducement to them at the time that I had any policy on the subject different from what I have laid down to-night. I pointed out to them on that occasion the advantages that the cities were enjoying over their country fellow-citizens outside the cities, and I gave them this hint : I said it had occurred to me that if the cities desired to have the rate on drop-letters reduced to one cent, the same as it is in places outside the cities, it would perhaps be reasonable that the cities
X
should pay for the advantage, and I think so to-day.
Has the hon. gentleman worked that idea out, or has it lain dormant since 7

I have not worked it out, but I dare say it would be possible to formulate a system by which we could keep track of the revenue collected in that way. It might be possible, but I fear it would be a very difficult task to keep an account of the volume of drop-letters posted in a city and to commute that in a certain sum payable by the city as a whole. That was the idea I suggested on that occasion, but as to saying -that I had at any time; favoured the reduction of the rate on drop-letters to that prevailing outside the cities, where the people do not enjoy the same advantages as in the cities, is an error ; I .never so expressed myself, I never had such an idea.
At any rate, you have no idea of that kind now.
I have not any idea of the kind now ; I do not think it is just; I do not think the great cities would press for such an unjust measure. They enjoy great advantages.

I do not want to enter into a discussion as to which of these rates should be lowered, but the minister a short time ago referred to the increased postage on books, and said that the revenue derived from that source would be trifling. I am aware that it is difficult for the minister or the officers of his department to find out just what that revenue is, but I cannot help thinking that if he had looked into the matter he would have found that the increase is so large as to amount to a very heavy tax.
Enormous.

It is not a matter in regard to which I have made inquiries outside my own business, but even in the business with which I am connected it makes a difference of several hundred dollars a year, and I would like to mention that. I am not complaining, as we are getting it out of our customers, but it amounts to several hundred dollars a year, and I know it has increased our postal rate by between 30 and 35 per cent.
What class of books 7

Catalogues and books or that kind. I presume every manufacturing house in the country will have a somewhat similar experience, and I mention it now to call the attention of the minister to it, because I cannot help thinking he is in error in believing that the amount is trivial. If it amounts to several hundred dollars in a comparatively small business, I think that

in the larger businesses it must amount to a very large sum indeed. As I said, I do not know that it is a cause of complaint. I have never felt inclined to complain myself, as we charge it up to expense and add it to the price of the goods, but if there is a revenue sufficient to justify a reduction in the postal rates, it seems to me it would be relieving a large number of people of rather a heavy tax if he could see his way clear to reduce the book rate to the old rate. The minister has said that the change was undoubtedly made because of the desire to bring the rate for the carriage of hooks and similar matter into fair proportion of the cost to the department of that carriage. That is what I understood the minister to say. I may say then that our experience has been that the book rate now is so high on catalogues and such matter that wherever we can send by the express company to within a good many hundreds of miles, it pays us to send by express. It is materially cheaper to send by express than by post, simply because the express companies have a special rate of 15 cents on such classes of goods, and 15 cents will carry a greater weight of catalogues by express than by postage. I mention that as a matter of information ; it is not a matter that I feel inclined to criticise one way or another. It is an open question as to whether the lates should be reduced, but I think that the amount of revenue is not trifling.

If the Postmaster Gen eral has any excess of revenue to expend on improving the service, my idea is to expend it in improving the parcel post system. We in Canada have a parcel post system somewhat better than that in the United States, but not to be compared with the parcel post systems in Europe, especially in Germany, Hungary and Great Britain. They have a much improved parcel ^post system there ; their rates are simply' fractional as compared with ours.
Have our parcel post rates been increased ?

I do not know that they have been increased. *The size of parcels has not been increased and the facilities offered to the public have not been increased, for the reason, I believe, that prevents these benefits from being conferred upon the people in the United States, and that is that the express companies in the United States are so powerful that they have prevented the extension of the parcel postal system in that country as I believe they have prevented it in this country. The business men of Canada would like us to use the parcel post system and they want the rates reduced and the size of the parcels increased. This has taken place in Europe. It has stimulated trade in every branch there and certainly we could bring about the same results here. Another way in which the post office could facilitate trade would Mr. LAVELL.
be to still further simplify the transmission of small amounts of money whether by postal notes or otherwise. We are making progress in that direction but in no way is our system for the carriage of small sums of money and parcels to be compared with the facilities in those directions afforded in Europe. The facilities afforded in Europe in that regard have stimulated trade in every direction and have enabled small tradesmen and people who wish to market their own products to get the best price possible for them. If the hon. the Postmaster General has any sui'plus and if he wishes to serve the Canadian people I would recommend to him that he study particularly the system of these European countries and use the money at his disposal in carrying it out as far as possible.
What is the difference in the price of postal orders here and in the old country ?
The price in the old country is only a fraction of what we pay here.
For what ?
Postal notes, and parcel post rates.
No.

I can give the hon. gentleman some instances of it. I would also suggest to the hon. gentleman that he might greatly simplify the law. The law might be greatly simplified if we improved. the parcel post system in this country. It is well worthy of consideration and that is in line with a matter that I have brought up before in this House in regard to express companies. They are too powerful. They have too much influence. They fight against any extension of the parcel post system and they are trying to keep up the rates. Let the Post Office Department in this country have the courage of the Post Office Department of Great Britain, Germany and Austria and greatly improve the parcel postal system. In that way the hon. Postmaster General can do a great deal for the people and greatly simplify the present system.
I would like to ask the hon. Postmaster General if he has looked into the question of the rural delivery system which has been quite a success on the other side.
Perhaps the committee will allow my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) to intervene with a matter that he desires to bring to the attention of the House and then we can resume.

The hon. Postmaster General can answer the question of my hon. friend from East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) later.

Sir WILLIAM MULOCIC Yes, in a few minutes.
