speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We have an item respecting the duty on artificial teeth which was the cause of some humorous observations. Perhaps hon. gentlemen will be surprised to know that it is an item which created a great deal of interest, and much importance is attached to it. We have reached the conclusion that the placing of artificial teeth on the free list should be deferred to a date to be mentioned, and the date we fix is the 1st day of April next. In the interim we propose to reduce the duty from 20 per cent to 10 per cent. It is represented to us that there are very large stocks of artificial teeth held in Canada, and indeed it is somewhat surprising to know the extent to which this is-the case. We knew it was a considerable item, but it is even larger than we anticipated and it is represented that the sudden placing of artificial teeth on the free list would have a very disturbing and unfair influence on merchants who hold large stocks. We therefore propose to bring about the change gradually, while adhering to the essence of the policy. There is another item which reads :
Table ware of porcelain, china, or other clay.
For the purpose of more clearly defining it, we insert the word ' white ' so that it will read :
Table ware of china, porcelain or other white clay.
This will prevent confusing the item with some others which were not intended.
There is a provision in the tariff of a year ago for the admission free of duty of machinery for the manufacture of sugar from beet root. That provision has expired, and we propose to renew it for the term of another year up to April next.
In the item of ' molasses,' which is placed on the free list when imported from countries entitled to the British preference, we wish to insert words which will stipulate that it must be a direct importation. The object of the government is to guard against molasses being landed abroad and mixed with other ingredients which people in the trade assure us is a practice which we ought very carefully to guard against.
We have placed on the free list the item of printing presses, and it has been deemed desirable that that should be more clearly defined. We propose that the item shall read :
Printing presses, rotary.
This will make it clear that other classes of printing presses which we did not contemplate, shall not be included in the item, and are not transferred to the free list.
There is one other matter which is of importance, and that is the date on which these various changes in the way of increased duties shall take effect. As a rule, under the practice in Canada, whenever the budget speech is delivered such changes of tariff as may be made take effect at once ; and as the resolution now stands without any qualification, that would be the result.. However, there are precedents for taking a different course. Some years ago. for good reasons no doubt, the operation of the new resolutions was delayed for a period, and in the case of the German surtax we adopted the same policy. Following these precedents, we now propose to provide : that in the case of all goods actually ordered before the date of the budget-and confining it entirely to goods so actually ordered-if they be entered in Canada on or before the last day of August next, they shall be admitted under the old rate of duty, and the new rate of duty shall only apply to cases in which the goods have not been ordered as provided. The reason for this is, that it has been represented that in some lines, notably woollen goods, large quantities were sold in advance at fixed prices on the basis of the existing duties. The goods in some cases were on their way and the orders could not be cancelled. After very careful consideration, we have come to the conclusion that no injury will be done the woollen industry, for which the benefit was intended, because the goods are ordered and have to come in any how. The only question is whether we should exact the higher duty. After full consideration we believe that in the case of all duties which have been increased by these resolutions- this will apply to the special duty as well as to the various items which are set forth- where the goods have been actually ordered on or before the 7th day of June, they shall come in at the old rate, provided they are entered in Canada on or before the last day of August. These. Mr. Speaker, are all the changes. The Votes and Proceedings will contain all the resolutions in their amended form, but, gentlemen who have read the resolutions as previously submitted, if they read them now In conjunction with this explanation, will be able to determine exactly the nature and purpose of the changes. In most cases the changes are very trivial, but as regards the date on which the increased duties take effect, that, is an important change, and I desired this opportunity to make it known amongst the trade all over the country which has been so anxious for a definite announcement upon the subject. I am obliged to the House for having kindly consented to allow me to put the matter in this form. There will be in connection with this, some necessary amendments to the Customs Act. The tariff is dealt with by an Act called the Customs Tariff. 1897 : apart from that there is the Customs Act which deals with the general management of the Customs Department. The Minister of Customs will have to make some amendments to that Act. My hon. friend will give notice of these amendments, but they are not of
Mr. FIELDING

sufficient importance to justify me in detaining tlie House at this moment.

May I say a few words with reference to the industry in which I am particularly interested. I am sure it is not the intention of the Minister of Finance to do any particular damage to the oil industry. Though I do not believe in the bounty system, yet as that has been decided upon I would like to call the attention of the minister to a few remarks I have to make with reference to the necessity of putting on a greater bounty than the minister proposes. As I said on a former occasion, the crude oil which comes from the Ohio fields is of a superior quality to ours. I have worked out 100 gallons of the imported crude oil through a refinery, and the result is that I got $1.03 in value more from Ohio oil than from 100 gallons of our own oil, showing it to be worth about one cent a gallon more than our oil. or say 35 cents per barrel. The oil is sold in Ohio at $1.08 per barrel, to which if you add the transportation charges for delivery at Sarnia of 23 cents it will make $1.31. If you add the 52 cents bounty as suggested, that comes to $1.83. At the time this change was made the difference between $1.83 and $2.09, left the balance in favour of the Ohio oil as compared with our own oil of 26 cents per barrel. Add to that 26 cents per barrel the 35 cents I referred to a moment ago being the extra value of the Ohio crude, and that makes a total preference for the Ohio oil of 61 cents per barrel. I beg to call the attention of the Minister of Finance to the fact, that not only is that giving an advantage of 61 cents to the Ohio oil, but it must be remembered that in Essex. Kent, Lambton and Elgin counties, the oil is gathered at a considerable distance from the Standard refinery, and that it costs a good deal to deliver it in the Standard tanks. Previous to this I have computed the values as if our oil were delivered in the Standard tanks at Sarnia. I have made a calculation with reference to the cost of gathering the oil in the Pretolea field and delivering it to the Standard refinery seventeen miles distant, and I have come to the conclusion that this costs ten cents per barrel. Therefore, as between the Ohio oil and our own oil it makes a difference against us of 71 cents per barrel. To the people in the outside districts, such as Bothwell, Dutton and the other oil fields from which the oil has to be sent to Sarnia by train it is a more serious matter, and I feel like drawing the attention of the Finance Minister to the importance of giving the producers of Canada sufficient protection against Ohio crude.

I desire to ask the Minister of Finance if there will be a rebate of duty allowed on goods which have been
passed through the customs since the 7th of June, and on which the higher duty has been paid ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, if there be evidence that the goods were ordered prior to that date, as of course they would have been, or I presume they would not be delivered. The goods actually ordered before the date of the 8th of June and entered before the end of August will not be subject to the higher duties, and if the duties in the meantime have been paid, they will be entitled to a rebate.

Then, I would like to point, out how difficult it is going to be to carry out the anti-dumping clause. I have received four circulars from manufacturers in the United States intimating that they would invoice goods into Canada at American prices, and would pay to Canadian dealers the same salary for handling their goods that they pay to American dealers. That will defeat the anti dumping clause altogether.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is not the time for debating that question. All I can say is that I have no doubt the Minister of Customs will find the means of meeting a case of that kind. We shall be only too glad to have such cases brought to our notice in order that we may look into them.

As an importer, I would like to know what would be the effecj, provided we Import goods at United States prices. Can they be passed through our customs at those prices when the manufacturer pays the importer a salary for disposing of the goods ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am afraid I cannot answer that question. In the administration of the customs laws a great many questions of that kind are brought up, and have to be dealt with as they arise from time to time.

Another question I would like to ask the Finance Minister. In the case of articles which formerly paid a duty, but are now imported free, on what date will they be entitled to come in free ? In other words, when does the law take effect-on the 7th or the 8th of June ?
Mr. IflELDING. I am afraid I had better not answer my hon. friend lest I get into trouble. We shall have all these questions discussed in due course.
I beg to ask an easy question. Perhaps the hon. minister can tell us on what day he will take up these resolutions. Will he take them up this week or next week ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I can give my hon. friend the assurance that they will not be taken up this week. They will come into

effect at once, and therefore I desire to make the announcement now ; but the discussion will take place later.
It makes no difference to me when they take effect. I want simply to know when we shall have an opportunity of discussing them, so that I may be present.

All this quibbling about the tariff shows the bad policy Canada is pursuing. I have no doubt those people in the United States will find the most ample opportunity of defeating the clause in the tariff that is proposed. My hon. friend the Finance Minister says the Minister of Customs will look after that. I have not the same faith in the Minister of Customs ; I think we shall have to have a new Minister of Customs if he is to possess ingenuity enough to prevent those people cheating the revenue of Canada. What we want in Canada is a tariff of the same height as the American tariff. Then there will be no question of quibbling with the tariff such as we have had to-night. For my part, I stand here as a maritime province man. Formerly the people of the maritime provinces were supposed to be in favour of free commercial relations with the United States. I stand here to say that the maritime provinces do not want any relations whatever with the United States. What*we want is a high tariff to exclude the manufacturers of the United States from this country. In the county of Colchester we have a great iron industry and the great complaint of the people connected with that industry is that $30,000,000 of manufactured iron comes into this country. We are prevented from building up our own industries because hon. gentlemen opposite, while professing to protect them, are allowing $30,000,000 of iron goods to come into this country and are offering these people a bonus. The bonus is only applicable to one or two lines of manufactured materials. Unfortunately they went to those parties in Cape Breton who are now face to face with financial embarrassment. The hon. gentlemen are killing their friends as well as their enemies-thank God.

Mr. Speaker, before you leave the chair, I wish to give notice that to-morrow, on the motion for the House to go into Committee of Supply, I will move this resolution :
This House regrets that the government has seen fit to withhold from parliament documents of a public character to which parliament was entitled for the proper consideration of matters to which such documents relate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
House in Committee of Supply.
Post Office-Outside service-Mail service, $2,561,700.

["I beg to lay cu the table of the House certain papers Sir WILLIAM MULOCK.\nthat were asked for by the hon. member '01' Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk), also my letter to Colonel Whitley, which was asked for by the leader of the opposition. It is a private letter, but I have obtained the consent of Colonel Whitley to lav it on the table."]

Before the committee rose an hon. member referred to the transmission of money by post in Great Britain. He mentioned that the parcel rate in Canada was greater than the parcel rate in European countries. That may be the ease, but the distances in Canada are very much greater. It would be impossible, with any regard to business, to carry parcels throughout Canada at the same rate that is charged in Great Britain. I suppose they are carried in Canada ten times the distance that they are in Great Britain. With reference to the rates on postal notes and the development of the postal note system, I have made a little comparison and I think it will be found that we are quite as reasonable in Canada as they are 1n England. The rate charged in England on a postal note up to Is. 6d., is a half-penny. In Canada the charge is one-half penny or a cent up to forty cents. In England the rate charged on a postal note from one shilling and six pence up to ten and six pence is a penny or two cents. In Canada the rate is two cents from fifty cents to two dollars and a half. In England the rate on postal notes exceeding ten and six and going up to twenty shillings is one and a half penny or three cents. In Canadla it is three cents' on a sum from three to five dollars. In England the postal note system stops at one pound, but in Canada we have got beyond that limit and our postal notes are issued for amounts as high as ten dollars, on which the rate is five cents. I do not think that the comparison of rates is to our disadvantage.

What I pointed out was that especially in Germany and Austria, *they have even a cheaper rate for postal notes than we have. As regards the postal parcel post system, the hon. gentleman might divide the country into zones, or if he cannot do that, some other means might be provided. But as a matter of fact, he is carrying parcels from the English parcel post system to any place in Canada for the rate that obtains in England, and he does this because of the postal convention. So that while he may object to doing that in connection with parcels originating in Canada, he must do it for parcels originating in Great Britain. In that way the English parcel post system applies in Canada to packages coming from England, and it is much cheaper than what we charge here and the parcels are much larger.
No.

I think they give you larger weight in England than here. I am
5T45

not complaining of the present system and willingly give the hon. gentleman credit for the improvement in the postal note service; but if there is a department in connection with the Post Office service which is subject to improvement, it Is, as far as I can gather from business men, the parcel post and postal note system.

I would like the hon. minister to answer this question. In 1890 the number of post offices in Canada was 7,930 and in 1896 that number had increased to 9,103, being an increase of 1,190 in the six years. From 1S96 to 1902 the increase was 855 or 335 less than in the previous six years. Would the hon. gentleman explain how that comes about ?

I do not wish to make any reflection, but post offices were opened with very great liberality in days gone by, and a considerable number of them became closed through lack of business. But the post offices in existence to-day are all live, working offices, and there is far more business being done in those in existence to-day than there was in the greater comparative number in existence when we took office. The country is not being starved, for lack of post offices. My daily task is to open up new post offices, and the case has to be a pretty bad one which does not appeal to me favourably. I think there will be found in the records very few applications for a post office, recommended by the inspector, which have not been granted. Ifa the year now closing, we have opened 310 new post offices throughout the Dominion and there are 83 now authorized, hut nob yet opened.
In what part of Canada ?

My hon. friend is probably aware that every application for a post office is referred to the inspector of the district, who makes a report describing the neighbourhood, the number of people to be served, the distance from another post office, the estimated cost, &c-In most cases the inspector gives his views and recommends whether or not the post office should be opened. I doubt whether during the current year five applications have been refused, which have been recommended by the inspectors. These new offices have been opened1 chiefly in the Territories, particularly in Saskatchewan. I recognize the importance of giving postal facilities to the settlers. When a man comes out to settle in this country and finds himself distant from railway communication, it is very important that he should be provided with postal facilities, and we have been very liberal, hut not too much so, in providing such facilities.

Is the hon. gentleman prepared to tell us whether he 'has made
any progress in nationalizing the telegraph and telephone system in connection with his department ?

That is a large question and I would like my hon. friend to ask me an easier one. I cannot say that I have made any great progress in the way of having anything to offer to parliament, but I hope that the educational movement is going on. I would hail with great pleasure the time when the telephone system would be taken under the wing of the government. My own opinion is in favour of some such course. I stated a year ago that I had been studying the subject, and so I have been.
Are you still studying it?

I cannot say that I am at this moment. I have formed, some views and have some figures, but I am not in a position now to give them to the House. I trust however the time will come when I shall be free to do so.

I would ask for information from the Postmaster General with reference to mail contracts, and I will introduce the subject now so that he may make the necessary inquiries. I refer to the mail between River John and the post office, and between River John and Hodson. I would liae to know who the mail carrier is, what he is receiving, and whether the contract was let after tenders called for or by private arrangement. For the item respecting the River John and the railway station I would refer him to page B-78 of his report, and for the other to B-71.
As to the former, the name given here is W. Gammon.
I think he has been replaced.

I will ascertain that point and also the others the hon. gentleman wished information about. The , remuneration in the case I have just referred to appears to be $58 a year. The Act allows the Postmaster General, where the remuneration for carrying the mail is less than $200, to make a contract without calling for tenders. Probably in so small a matter tenders would not be called for. But I will get the information for my hon. friend.
When ?
To-morrow, if he will remind me.

I desire to ask a question with regard to the St. Thomas post office. The deputy postmaster there died some two weeks ago. What progress is the hon. minister making with respect to filling that position ?

I am sorry to say that the assistant postmaster of St.

Thomas died a few days ago. I hope to be able to fill the place by promotion from that office.

I would like to say also that iu my opinion the staff is not adequate for the business of the office. It should be increased.
'Sir WILLIAM MULOCK. That may fol-.ldw. But I thought the bon. gentleman (Mr. Ingram) was particularly concerned to know who was to be given this particular position. As to that, I will look into the staff and if there is one among them whom it would be proper to promote to the assistant postmastership, I would rather fill the pffice in that way. It may be necessary also to add to the staff.

During the summer months the clerks in the office take their holidays, and the effect of that is to leave them one clerk short for some months. I think the Postmaster General should give this matter his serious attention, and provide an ample staff for the requirements of the office.

I had occasion last year to call the attention of the Postmaster General to the unfair treatment meted out to Charlottetown in the matter of free mail delivery. While smaller towns throughout Ontario were having the benefit of delivery by letter-carriers, Charlottetown was denied that advantage. I think that when this matter was before the committee last year the Postmaster General gave us the assurance that he would take the matter up and favourably consider it. I would like to know if he has made any progress in that matter.
I do not know to what towns in Ontario the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lefurgey) refers.
We had them up last year. I cannot call them off now, but no question was raised about it then.

I am afraid that our friends from Ontario would rather take issue with the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lefurgey) on that point. There is no town in Ontario as small as that of Charlottetown that enjoys free delivery. The towns that have the benefit of that system now are Ottawa, Kingston, Toronto, Hamilton, Brantford and London. I think that, on reference to the postal returns, the hon. gentleman will find that every one of these places has a revenue larger than that of Charlottetown. Speaking from memory, the revenue from Charlottetown does not exceed $19,000, while I think that the revenue from Brantford is nearly $35,000. Probably the next revenue is that of Kingston, but it is some thousands in excess of Charlottetown. However, Charlottetown is growing and the place is improving, and I agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Lefurgey) in the hope that it Sir WILLIAM MULOCK.
will continue to make rapid progress until its claims for free delivery will be unanswerable.

That is very plausible talk, but not just what we want. We want free delivery. When I brought this matter up last year the hon. Postmaster General seemed to be favourably impressed with the claims of Charlottetown for free delivery. I cannot recall the names of places brought to his attention that had a smaller population than Charlottetown and yet enjoyed this free delivery system. .This system should not be given on the basis of revenue only ; population should be considered. Where you have the people you are bound to give the service. And, as the coffers of the hon. minister are, apparently overflowing, I think he could fairly do justice to places of the population of Charlottetown.
What is its population ?
Upwa'rds of from 12,000 to 15,000 people, and growing, growing all the time.
That is always a good sign.

Joking aside, the people down there I think deserve a free delivery by letter-carriers, and a great deal better treatment than they are getting at the present time. I would like to know from the minister if the post office inspector for the island has been appointed and if so, what salary he is getting. Is the arrangement the same as with the old inspector ?
Yes. Mr. Weir was appointed in the place of the late postmaster and inspector, Mr. Breeken, at I think the same salary.
No changes were made in the office ?
No change in the duties or salary.
I would like to know from the Postmaster General if he had any petitions in regard to a daily service at lot 14 post office, and whether anything has been done for the people in that locality ?
I will make a note of my hon. friend's inquiry and give him the information to-morrow.

I would like also to inquire about a post office for North Enmore. This is a small village three or four miles from any post offiee, and have on two occasions made applications for a post office and promises have been made, possibly by the inspector of post offices, in Prince Edward Island but nothing has been done. There is quite a large settlement that should be served by a post office. I would like

also to know wliat arrangements were made for the carriage of mails from Cape Tormen-tine to Sackville, and if the contract has been carried out and payment made to the persons who had that contract. I asked a question some time ago about this, and the reply then was that no arrangement had been made with the people who were carrying the mails from Oape Tormentine to Sackville. I thought it was a very strange proceeding that a contract should have been entered into by the government whereby these people were to go ahead and carry the mails without any agreement at all. I would like to know what the arrangement was.
iSir WILLIAM MTILOCK. Was that arrangement made during the winter season last year ?
Yes.
There was I think some special difficulty in the service on account of ice.
I believe there was a block on the railway system.
It is a special service growing out of the storm, is it not ?
I presume so, there is always some difficulty there about getting the mails across the strait.
It has puzzled more than one person. I shall have all this information gathered up and shall give it to my hon. friend to-morrow.

The Postmaster General said a while ago that post offices were granted on the recommendation of the inspector of post offices. Will the hon gentleman be kind enough to tell the committee what recommendation the Quebec inspector made with regard to the proposed post office at Detroit, in the county of Dorchester ? Has he recommended it or condemned it ?
I think the hon. gentleman saw the report, he will remember, I do not know from memory.
I did not see it.
I shall examine the report and let the hon. gentleman know to-morrow.
Thank you.

Some time ago I inquired about the post office at Wolford centre. I believe that the difficulty in connection with the office there is practically causing the post office to be closed. That would be a tremendous inconvenience to a body of farmers not now served by any other convenient office. I would ask the minister to look into that with the idea of restoring the service as it was. I think since 1896 there
has been a better service, but on account of some change in mail carriage a proposal was made to change it to a twice-a-week service, which would produce an annual saving of $20.

I think I remember having seen a report of the inspector on that matter. I think it is rather a tangled affair and that there are some differences of opinion on the subject among the people. I shall be glad to discuss the subject with my hon. friend to see whether it is possible to meet all interests.

There was some difficulty about a year or two ago, but I think they all recognize now what an inconvenience the closing of the office will mean, and they are absolutely united now in regard to seeing the post office kept open as it was.
I shall go through the papers with my hon. friend and get the benefit of his advice.

Might I_ ask the minister what has been done with" reference to rural free delivery in our country. I am satisfied that the hon. gentleman is aware that rural free delivery in the United States is wonderfully successful. It has become so through continued efforts and I should like to know what has been done in this country.

I do not know what my hon. friend means when he says that rural delivery in the United States has been successful. It may be that there is no difficulty in delivering the mail matter but there are more things than the mere delivery of mail matter required in order to make a system a success. The United States people were rather dragooned into the establishment of rural mail delivery and it has rafted very serious problems in the United States. 1 venture to say that in the very .near future there will be a feeling in the United States that they were rather rash in rushing into that system. In fact that feeling has already arisen. My own opinion is that Canada is not ripe for the establishment of rural mail delivery at the present time. It is only a few years since the United States entered that scheme.
How were the United States dragooned into this system ?

It is only a few years since the United States started that system and now the expenditure has risen to about $12,000,000 and is going in the near future to be many times that amount. For some time the officers throughout the country engaged in working the system represented it as a huge success, and succeeded in having those views certified to in the official reports of the Postmaster Gen: eral of the United States. I think that more

recent information has shown that there were many inaccuracies in the returns made to the Postmaster General of the United States and that the system has not been that success which those who were engaged in developing it and who profited by its development represented.
Nevertheless, it has acquired a footing today throughout the United States. Practically every candidate for congress pledges himself to get rural delivery in his constituency, and when the successful ones meet at Washington they are all engaged in demanding rural delivery. The unfortunate administration is evidently at its wits end to know what to do with this monster that has been raised up, and has apparently no way of controlling the thing. I believe that those who are concerned with the affairs of the government at Washington find a serious condition of affairs growing up in the United States in reference to rural delivery. Moreover, there is evidence that in many parts of the country it is not now as popular as it was originally. It sounds very taking to say that a man is going to have his mail brought to his farm gate, but when you come to work it out there is another side to the picture. For example, supposing a mail route commences half a mile from the village or town, goes ten miles into the country in one direction, crosses a concession, goes down in another direction and covers a distance of twenty-five miles. The courier commences at one end and terminates his journey at the other. He starts off at a reasonable hour, about the time that those who are nearest to the town could have gone to the post office and got their mail. Those at the commencement of the route are all right, but those situated farther along the route do not get their mail until perhaps late in the night. Many who go to the post office once or twice in the day or in the week, as the mails come in, find themselves inconvenienced when their letters are taken off by the courier, thus showing that the inconvenience to one man off-sets the advantage to another. The question of rural delivery in a country of the vast size of the United States is giving serious concern to the public men of that enormously wealthy country. Imagine the Post Office Department undertaking to serve the people of this young country, with an area equal to that of the United States, in the same way as is done in smaller countries, such as England and in Europe. Fancy the establishment of a rural delivery system within an area the size of all Europe. That is what is involved in proposing to adopt rural delivery in Canada, and the first step of the Postmaster General would be to ask the House to vote $5,000,000 or $10,000,000, perhaps not the first year, but in a very short time. The first year perhaps $1,000,000 or $2,000,000 would be sufficient, bat it would go on so that in five years the Postmaster General would have to ask the House Sir WILLIAM MULOCK.
to give $10,000,000 or $15,000,000 to establish rural delivery. Parliament would not be in favour of voting that sum of money. I doubt if the country could afford that amount of money. It might be that in a few years we would be called upon to vote an item of probably not less than $25,000,-
000.	The figures are alarming and disturbing, and therefore I do not think the country is prepared to adopt this system at the present moment.
How much did the hon. gentleman say ?
In a few years the cost might be $25,000,000.
What is the total vote now ?

$4,500,000. I think the amount the United States congress voted last year was $12,000,000 and odd. To show you how they have miscalculated, their figures were based on the theory that a courier could be found to carry these mails on a route from 20 to 25 miles in length, supply his own horse and vehicle, and do it for $500 a year. Their figures are based on $500 to each man. The couriers said, after they got the system started, that they could not afford to carry on the system at that rate, and they wanted an increase. But they had to deal with a man who is even more hard-hearted than the Postmaster General of Canada, and they were denied the increase. Thereupon they undertook to supplement their salaries by .carrying merchandise and doing an express and passenger traffic. Then persons engaged in the express and pa'ssenger traffic protested against this, and the authorities, in the endeavour to prevent the carriage of passengers and express parcels, granted the request of the couriers and raised their fees from $500 to $750 a year. Immediately a dislocation of their calculations by 50 per cent took place. Now, the couriers are not satisfied and they are agitating to have their salary increased to $1,000 a year. If this demand is granted, the calculations upon which they based the whole proposal originally given to congress will be upset to the extent of 100 per cent. They have taken hold of a problem which is alarming, and one which no prudent government would think of adopting in Canada at the present time. My deputy Informs me that the vote they are asking this year from congress is $17,000,000.
They started with a vote of how much ?
Less than

The hon. Postmaster General, in reply to a statement made by my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) this afternoon, said that in the Montreal post office letter-carriers are not required

to work more than eight hours a day, and that if they do work more than eight hours the extra time is allowed on the following day or on some succeeding day. Is that correct 1
That is correct.
Does the same rule apply in Toronto ?
The letter-carriers in Toronto, I am told, do not do any extra work.
How many hours do they work ?
Eight hours.
If they work more than eight hours, what then ?

My deputy informs me that the question has never arisen. Eight hours is the time. Until a recent date there was no limit to the hours of their service ; they were required to work as long as there was work to do, whether it was nine or ten hours a day. I thought it was only right to fix a limit to a day's work, and I have fixed eight hours as the extent of a day's work.
What does a day's work include ?
A day's work means the eight hours that they are on duty.
Sorting letters and all that ?
Yes.
I understand they work eight hours a day, and if they are obliged to work a longer period they will be allowed that time or get paid for it ?

Yes. The question has not arisen in Toronto, because they are not required to work over eight hours. They are paid by the day and if the men were called upon to do any extra work exceeding eight hours, that time would be credited to them in the near future.
I am glad to hear that.
The aim is to have eight hour service.
There is no doubt about it that if they work more than eight hours they will be allowed the time, or get extra pay for it ?
That is the spirit in which we are dealing with it.
And that rule will be carried out in the spirit in which the minister has presented it to us ?
Yes. In a service like the post office it is of course impossible to adhere to fixed hours at all times.
The working time of these men is limited to eight hours per day ?
These are my instructions.
That is the rule now ?
That is the rule.
And if there is any violation of that rule the minister will see that the men are compensated, or allowed time ?
It will be compensation if they are allowed time.
How many letter-carriers have accepted the new scheme which the minister has evolved, and abandoned the old plan under which they entered the service ?
Under the extension of time granted by parliament last year, sixty-eight letter-carriers throughout the Dominion came in.
How many declined to come in ?
It is not a matter of declining ; it is an option. I will bring down the information to the hon. gentleman with reference to the city of Toronto, and if he wishes in regard to the rest of Canada.

It would be interesting to know that.
-Sir WILLIAM MULOCK. Will the hon. gentleman be good enough to state the precise information he needs, and I will have it furnished ?
I am much obliged to the Postmaster General. There were some superior officers of the department going around amongst these men and pointing out that they should come in
That is a mistake.

The minister may not be personally aware of it, but it is a fact all the same. If these men prefer to remain under the old system they should be allowed to do so. Might I ask the minister if any petitions have been received by him from the men who are in this new scheme, as well as from the old men, for an increased wage, and what was done with the request ?

My hon friend is entirely in error in supposing that there is the slightest pressure on the part of the government, the Postmaster General or any officer, to induce any letter-carriers to avail themselves of this privilege. I told the hon. gentleman so last-session ; I tell him so again and he ought be assured. This is a

measure that some people would think for the advantage of the letter-carriers, and it is entirely in their discretion to avail of it or not. It is no great advantage to the government to have to pay a letter-carrier $125 more than he is now drawing. I am not gaining anything by his coming under the system ; it was designed for their benefit and while some have stood out others have come to the conclusion that it is to their benefit to come in.
Quite a number do not see it in that light.

They may not, and it is not necessary that they should see it in that light, so far as we are concerned. Some of them are now asking to avail of the privilege. My bon. friend does an injustice to some of the officers in the Toronto post office, when he suggests that any of them are busying themselves to advise the letter-carriers. I am aware, that there are some people engaged in always trying to make mischief amongst the letter-carriers in the city of Toronto, and misleading them and making them feel they are down-trodden and abused. I heard this story that someone was endeavouring to coerce them, and I made it my business to make inquiries myself, and I went to the city post office. I called upon the chief superintendent, Mr. Lemon-I do not know that I need mention names. I asked him if he were aware of any person trying to induce the letter-carriers to come in under the new system, and he said : no ; that many of them had come in under it and that others were considering it, and that some who did not come in Were seeking advice as to what was in their interests and they had asked some other officials to give them advice. I asked him the name of any persons who had been giving him opinions, and he gave me the name of a very worthy officer in the post office who had. been consulted by some of the letter-carriers and to whom he gave his opinion. I sent for that gentleman and asked him to explain to me what occurred and he said that some of the letter-carriers asked him his opinion and he felt it his duty to tell them frankly that if he were in their position he would consider the Act an advantage to him and he would avail himself of its privilege. That is the extent to which he gave them advice, and he gave it to them at their request. It was a matter of perfect indifference to him whether they acted upon it or not. Some of them have asked to have an Act now passed extending the time so that they may come in under it. They are intelligent men, but it is just a question to my mind whether or not we should again open the Act and let them in. Some of them have been wanting me to do it, and I am inclined to do it, but I have not reached a conclusion. I am informed that there are requests from eighteen letter-carriers in Toronto arid from twenty-two in Montreal asking that the Act be amended Sir WILLIAM MULOCK.
so as to enable them to avail themselves of the privilege.
Is the document containing these requests a confidential one ?
I should not think so.
Will the minister bring it down when he is bringing the balance of the correspondence ?
Yes. I shall do so on my supplementaries.
I understood the minister to say that he would bring it down tomorrow ?
I expect to get through these estimates to-night.
Of course, I do not know about that.
Well, I think it is only reasonable, and there will be sup-plementataries.
The minister will bear testimony to the fact that I have been assisting him all evening to get his estimates through.
I would like v to be saved from such assistance.
Has the minister received any memorials for increased remuneration from those letter-carriers who are in this new scheme ?
I really do not know ; certainly I would not grant it.
Will the hon. gentleman bring down that correspondence along with the other communications he received, and the replies he sent to these communications ?
I do not remember whether there is any correspondence on that point or not. If there are any applications I will bring them down ; I will bring the whole Post Office Department down.

There is a large item, amounting to about $30,000, for the supply and repair of mail bags. Is that work done by contract ?
Sir WILLIAM MUiLOCK. The mail bags are manufactured under contract. The contractor is a man named Carson, on Rideau street. The contract is for four years.
Mr. BEiLL. How are the repairs effected ?
An allowance per bag is made. Some bags are damaged more than others, and the allowance has to be averaged.

Has the Postmaster General received a petition from the railway mail clerks of Manitoba and the Territories, ask-

ing for an increase in their allowances ?
I have a copy of a petition which I understand was presented to him. These men claim that increases have been made to postmasters and others, and they think they are entitled to some consideration in that respect. They are a body of men scattered all over Manitoba and the Territories, and possibly they have not the influence that others may have; but they are a most important body, and take the greatest risks in regard to their lives. Their petition, I think, should receive the earnest consideration of the minister. I would like to ask him what he has to say in regard to it ?
My deputy informs me that no such petition has been deceived.

I have received a letter, dated Winnipeg, January 15, 1904, which says that at a largely attended meeting of the railway mall clerks it was unanimously decided to petition the Postmaster General for an increase. It is not very likely that such a letter would be sent to me if the petition had not been forwarded. I think the memory of the deputy minister is at fault.

I have not only the evidence of the deputy, but that of the controller also. If such a petition had been received by the department, the secretary would have at once transmitted it to the controller. I certainly am not prepared to increase the allowances to the railway mail clerks at the present time. They are liberally treated, and they fully appreciate it. Some busybody amongst them may have agitated for something more, but I am not prepared to yield to demands of that kind at the present time.
I do not know who these people may be, but here is the letter.' I have not busied myself about the matter at all.
I do not allude to the hon. gentleman.

The railway mail clerks will know now what the answer of the minister . is if they have not received it before. It is strange that this should be sent to me and no petition forwarded to the minister. I had probably better read the letter, so that it will go on ' Hansard ' :
Winnipeg, Man., Jan. 15, 1904.
Sir,-At a largely attended meeting of the Railway Mail Clerks Association of the Manitoba and Northwest Territories district, it was unanimously decided to petition the honourable the Postmaster General asking that he be pleased to increase the provisional allowance of the railway mail clerks of this district from 510 or 10 per cent as now given, to $15' per month.
As you are well aware, no doubt, the increase in the cost of living in this country has been very marked in the last year or two,
so much so, that the clerks feel justified in asking for this increase.
The honourable the Postmaster General has been pleased to grant a like increase to the clerks in city post offices in Manitoba and British Columbia, and the railway mail clerks consider that if the post office clerks are entitled to an increased allowance, they are equally, if not more so, to the same increase owing to the greater cost of living on account of being absent from their homes so much.
We are taking the liberty of asking all the members of parliament in our district to give us their aid and support in this matter and trust that you may be pleased to use your influence with the Postmaster General in our behalf.
We are, sir,
Your humble servants,
The Railway Mail Clerks Association,
Manitoba and N.W.T. district.
J. G. NORRIS,	CHAS. A. HISLOP,
President.	Secretary.

The reason I am not prepared to accede to any demands of the railway mail clerks at the present time is this. Last year parliament passed an Act very greatly benefiting the state of the railway mail clerks, and they fully understand and appreciate it. At the present time a railway mail clerk in Manitoba or the Northwest can go up to $1,200 a year, his mileage averages $500 a year, and he gets, in addition, an extra allowance of $120 a year, so that when he reaches the maximum he receives about $1,800 a year. The taxpayers have something to say on these questions, and I am not prepared to encourage every unreasonable demand for an increase. If it were shown that the men were not fairly remunerated, that would be another matter. The railway mail clerks are well remunerated, and they are I trust satisfied. There was one man who was a busybody, and made himself officious in trying to induce them to make further demands ; but he was repudiated by the well-thinking men some of whom published in the press their repudiation of his agitation. He came down here and called on me, and I pointed but to him what I thought was the unwise part he was playing. There was no desire on the part of the great body of the mail clerks for what he was trying to force upon them, and, in view of what had been done for them, his agitation for a further increase was very unseemly. I dare say he may have met some of these people and tried to organize them to pass some such resolution, and that letter was sent to my hon. friend ; but, on reflection, they may have thought better of it. At any rate, their views on that occasion were never communicated to the department.
Has the minister not called in the services of the fair-wage offi-j cer to settle disputes of this kind ?

I have the parliament of Canada to aid me in that matter,.

and X think we may depend on parliament being as wise as the fair-wage officer.

Then the services of that officer have not been called in ?
Sir t\ 1LLIAM MULOCK. I do not think parliament appointed him the adviser of this House.

I thought he might advise the hon. gentleman as to the rate of wages. Might I ask the Postmaster General what became of those automobiles which we used to see touring the streets of Toronto some years ago V
Some are worn out and some are still in use.
Are they abandoned altogether ?

We are going to abandon the system of automobiles when those in use become unfit for service.
Some resolutions reported.
Mr. FIELDING moved the adjournment of the House.
What business will be taken up to-morrow ?

Before you leave the chair, Mr. Speaker, I beg leave to move the following resolution :-
That this House regrets that the government has seem tit to withhold from parliament documents of a public character to which parliament was entitled for the proper consideration of -the matters to which such documents relate.

In support of this resolution, it may be necessary for me to deal with several questions which have come before this House within the last couple of years. The first matter with which I shall deal, is a certain memorandum prepared last session by a gentleman who was then a member of the cabinet, but which was not given to parliament on the plea that it was a confidential document intended for the sole information Of the government. A question then had come up, perhaps the most important this country has had to deal with for many years, the question of building a railway from the Pacific to the Atlantic. One of the members of the cabinet at the time differed from his colleagues with regard to the policy which ought to be adopted on that question. He prepared a document in which he set forth his views and gave that document to his colleagues. That document his colleagues treated as confidential, solely intended for themselves. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that when a minister of the Crown designs office because he cannot agree with his colleagues, on a question of policy this House is entitled to everything of a documentary character relating to that resignation. But my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, speaking on behalf of the government, took an entirely different view. He said that the document, in which his former colleague had stated his reasons for resigning, was confidential, intended only for the members of the government, and that any one who would make use of it so long as the seal of confidence was not removed, was just as guilty as the receiver of stolen goods. You all know the reference which the hon. gentleman then made to my . hon. friend the leader of the opposition. 1 hope that the Finance Minister has learned better since then. I hope he has learned that a document of that kind-no matter what term you may apply to it, private or secret or anything else-is one which the people are entitled to have and which the government were bound to disclose to the people, irrespective of the consent of the sender. But it must always be remembered that all public transactions of state are necessarily official ; and that no public officer would be justified in withholding from official record and access, any document, emanating from himself in his official capacity, in relation to public affairs.	[DOT]
