No document printed by a minister of the Crown who parts from his colleagues explaining why he differed from them on so 'important a question as the construction of a main line of transportation across the country can be considered a secret document. Nor can there be any justification for refusing to put the House in possession of a petition wbicb is .evidently intended for the Governor General, and which proposes a method of building a railway concerning which the people are exercised to a greater extent than they ever were before by the proposed construction of a public work. Yet these lion, gentlemen opposite concealed from the House for eighteen months the fact that this document was in existence, a document in the form of a petition, and formally praying in two or three places, and especially in the concluding part of it, that the government will take their petition into serious and favourable consideration. This, we are told, is to be treated as a confidential document, as one concerning which the people Mr. HAGGART.
must not be informed, when they are considering the most important question that has been before then for years. According to any reasonable theory of responsible government, the government is a committee of parliament, with parliament as a consultative body. And, on every, occasion parliament should be given the fullest information on everything that they are called upon to decide. But now, we, who at one time were ' democrats to the hilt ' have adopted what was alleged to be the oldi Tory practice of government by council, and keeping from the people information which they are entitled to-everything to be done under the cloak of ' private ' and ' confidential,' and parliament to be given, for assistance of its deliberations, not such information as is necessary to the interest of the country hut such as is deemed advisable in the interest of the government. We are told that the Conservative party, the great party of the past, is on the downward grade at the present day. How do you dare to accuse the Conservative party of taking a downward course ? And does not such an accusation come well from the party that never yet in power kept a pledge that it had made in opposition ? What charge of that kind can be made against the Conservative party ? None ; they have at least retained their honour. And better it would be to remain in opposition for centuries than to obtain power by false promises and' retain it without carrying out a single promise made in opposition. These gentlemen accuse us of being on the downward course. It reminds me of the famous answer of Cicero :	Clodius me aecusat. This
accusation that the Conservative party is moving downward comes from a party steeped in degradation-for there is no greater degradation than that of the man who says one thing and does another, who promises one thing and performs another, charging us with going downwards ! You may strain the English language, you may get the hon. member for Hants to give a meaning to a word which it does not bear and immediately after listening to it state that you did not intend to do it, that you intended to use another word. The hon. gentleman may refer to authority after authority in support of it but bis argument reached its sublimity when he told us of the Englishman going up to Scotland and being called a stranger on his arrival. The right hon. gentleman quoted Sir Walter Scott in support of his version of the meaning of ' stranger.' He little understands Sir Walter Scott, he little understood what Sir Walter Scott was writing about in reference to the Highlands of Scotland. Sir Walter Scott knew the Highland character well. An Englishman although newly arrived there, (Was an Englishman, a foreigner, an enemy, a Sassenach. The most contemptuous manner in which he could speak

of an Englishman on his arrival there was to call him a stranger. I thought when the right lion, gentleman quoted Sir Walter Scott that he was going to cite to us the lines which we all remember learning when we were boys, the description of tfie battle <>f the Saxon and the Gael where the High-landman concludes by presenting his sword to Fitz James, clasping it to his breast and saying :
Stranger, I am Roderick Dhu.
The right hon. gentleman may be right in ^ the meaning he attaches to the word, and' in quoting Sir Walter Scott. We do not win1 elections by matters of that kind, hut the right hon. gentleman must remember that on a celebrated occasion when Sir Charles Tupper ma.de a slip in reference to the right hon. gentleman in a speech delivered, I think in Winnipeg, and which he afterwards tried to explain, the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) held him firmly to the words which he uttered at that time. If the right "noil, gentleman holds others to their words

I would like to ask the hon. gentleman a question. Is he not mistaken in his reference to Fitz James and Roderick Dhu. Are not the closing words :
These are Clan Alpine's warriors true ;
And,-Saxon,-I am Roderick Dhu.
Not ' stranger.'
It is all the same..

It is all the same. It is ' stranger ' in my edition. I was dealing with the question with which the hon. gentleman was dealing the other evening. We will give him all the hope he wants in reference to that expression. I suppose we must take it for granted that the right hon. gentleman was thinking in one language and speaking in another and that he had difficulty in expressing his thoughts, and we are willing to accept his explanation that he did not mean the word he used. Both of them were offensive enough, goodness knows. As I said he must expect very little quarter ; we are at war with the right hon. gentleman and it is not war to let him out of his difficulties as easily as he expects to be let out. He did not let us out when-i ever an opportunity presented itself, and when Sir Charles Tupper made a slip yon heard of it from Quebec to the Pacific ocean. Sir Charles Tupper on one occasion called the right Cron, gentleman, a Frenchman and a Roman Catholic and said ' can you not expect more from me, a Protestant, in dealing with separate schools, than from a gentleman who is French and a Roman Catholic.' We caught it for that, from one end of the country to the other. The right hon. gentleman made the best use of it he could and he must expect in the war which we
are carrying on with him that we will take every means to remove him from power. Instead of the Conservative party going down, down, down, the right hon. gentleman and his party are going down, down, downwards. A few weeks from now there Will not he the cheering that we heard from the seats behind the hon. gentleman ; there will be a different tone. I much mistake the sentiment of this country at the present moment, or the time has come when these gentlemen who have been false and recreant to every promise they made to the people of this country when they had an opportunity of carrying out these promises will be repudiated by the people of the country who will become sick and tired of theiri extravagance, the false promises and the neglect to avail themselves of opportunities which presented themselves. When the opportunity arrives for an expression of public opinion I much mistake the sentiment of the country, I much mistake the sentiment of my- countrymen who are the backbone of the country which party the hon. gentleman leads. I mean the Scotchmen of the country if they do not repudiate the hon. gentleman. Above all tilings the Scotchmen are true to the empire, above all things they are true to a man of honour ; they are true to the man who they think has stood-, up for their rights and who has been unjustly deprived of a position from no neglect or indifference on his part but simply on a question -of etiquette between himself and the Minister of Agriculture.
I have been a member of this House for a number of years and I have never seem such treatment given to the House by the government in reference to the production of papers as we have had for the last two or three years. I regret the tone of this debate, I regret it because the ministers who manage the affairs of the country are responsible for it. I regret the tone of the debates in this House and I should like to! see a higher standard. The ministry should, keep the debates strictly within reasonable bounds ; they are responsible for the good conduct and honour of the House. I regret the cheapening effects which have ensued since these hon. gentlemen came into power and I hope for a better state of affairs.
I shall conclude my remarks by saying that I think I have proved up to the hilt that this House has been denied papers to which it has been entitled and which were necessary for the proper consideration of the subjects under discussion, and which do not come under the category of private, secret and confidential. These were papers to which the House is entitled, and it is our duty-because the privileges _ and rights of this House are the foundations of the liberties of the people of this country, to speak up and insist on every right which they possess. Where the publication of a

document does no injury to the individual privately, where it exposes no one to contumely, does no injury to the country by exposing some of its weakness In defence, but on the contrary would furnish information which might be to the benefit of the country, it then is the duty of the government to ask a grand inquest of the people, to trust in them, to consult with them and to give them all the information which is necessary for the proper consideration of the subject in hand.

Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to follow my hon. friend from South Lanark (Mr. Haggart) upon many o'f the questions which he has brought to the attention of-not to the attention of-but before the House, which have little if any relevancy to his motion. The subject might be a tempting one, but on the whole, I think it better, in view of the hope that he has expressed that the tone of this debate shall be higher than it has been in some debates of the past, that I should not attempt to follow everything that he has said. I will confine myself strictly to the object of this motion. Let me make one remark now to my hon. friend. He says that I cannot expect any quarter from his side of the House. Let me tell him that I never asked for any quarter, nor do I ask for any now. Provided the war is carried on, as it must be carried on, in the political sense, I mean, by honourable methods, I have nothing to complain of.
I will come at once to what is the object of the motion of my hon. friend. It is that the House shall censure the government for not having communicated to it certain information which was in its archives. My hon. friend confined his ground of attack to three different documents, that is to say, to the memorandum which Mr. Blair prepared upon the transportation question when he was a member of the government, to a certain letter addressed by Mr. Hays to the government upon the subject of the building of a transcontinental railway, and to the report of Lord Dundonald addressed by him to my hon. friend the Minister of Militia and Defence (Sir Frederick Borden). In regard to the first one of these documents the memo, prepared by Mr. Blair some two years ago, while he was a member of the government, upon the question of transportation generally, if I understood my hon. friend aright, he stated that this document should have been placed in the hands of the House. First of all since my hon. friend has referred to the fact that the tone of the debate is not as high as it was at one time, let me ask him :	How does he know that Mr. Blair
ever prepared any such document as that ? If he knows of it, it is not because he has had any information from us.

Because the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) and other Mr. HAGGART.
members of your own government have admitted it.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance).
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Haggart) is wrong. The Minister of Finance made no such admission.

As far as my memory serves me, my hon. friend the Minister of Finance never alluded to that document at all, but that document found its way into this House in a manner which still remains unexplained ; at all events* it did not come to the knowledge of the House in a manner that is consistent with the honour or forms of parliamentary debate, if we are able to keep up the dignity of debate which my hon. friend appears so anxious to do. The fact has gone abroad, it is a matter of public knowledge that Mr. Blair, when a member of this government offered to his colleagues a memo, on the subject of transportation. My hon. friend is an old parliamentarian, he has been many years in this House, he has been for several years a member of the government, and adviser of the Crown, and he knows that all communications of that character are strictly secret and confidential and that it is not in the power of any member of the administration to give out or discuss the contents of that document outside of the cabinet itself. It is true that Mr. Blair differed from his colleagues on the question of transportation. As a result of the dissent of Mr. Blair upon that question, he thought it advisable to withdraw from the government, and to place his resignation in the hands of His Excellency the Governor General. When he had placed his resignation in the hands of the Governor General, it was not only his duty, but it was his right and his privilege to give to the House all the information which he thought himself entitled to give in regard to the disagreement that had taken place between himself and his colleagues. He could not do so until he had obtained the permission and leave of the Governor General, leave which, under such circumstances is always given as a matter of course. When Mr. Blair took the view which he finally carried out of withdrawing from the government, he obtained from the Governor/ General permission to state to the House the causes of his disagreement which had led to the severing of his connection with his colleagues. He obtained upon that occasion leave to communicate to the House all the information which in his judgment was necessary and advisable to place the House in possession of the points of difference between him and his colleagues. Mr. Blair made his statement before the House, but Mr. Blair did not think it advisable to ask the Governor General for permission to lay that document before the House. If Mr. Blair had thought it advisable for his own protection and for the proper understanding of his position before

the country to ask His Excellency the Governor General for permission to place that document before the House, there is no doubt whatever that His Excellency would have given that permission, since, in justification to Mr. Blair himself who was the best judge of that matter, he thought the production of such a document to be essential to his defence. But Mr. Blair did not think it advisable ; he thought this communication which he had laid before his colleagues should remain what it was then and what it has been since-purely confidential, and under such circumstances, I say that I am still at a loss to understand upon what ground the House can ask for the production of that document as a public one. There can be no possible doubt as to that and upon this point, I think it is sufficient to make these observations to satisfy the House that the position of my hon. friend is absolutely untenable.
My hon. friend has mentioned another document-the letter of Mr. Hays, addressed to me personally as the head of the government, upon the question of building another transcontinental railway. We had a discussion upon this subject some time ago, and if my hon. friend will permit me to say so without offence, I think lie will agree with me that he has not added anything to the light which was thrown upon the subject by the observations he has made to-day.
Therefore, as my hon. friend has adduced no new argument upon this point, I will pass away from it without any further comment.
Then, 'my hon. friend came to the report of Lord Dundonald. I followed my hon. friend very closely upon that, especially when he made the statement in the early part of his remarks that he would give chapter and book which would conclusively show that a document of that character was in its nature a document which should have been made public immediately it had been placed in the hands of the Minister of Militia. My hon. friend spoke with greater emphasis as to the knowledge which he had upon this point, than the speech which he delivered warranted. X followed him very closely. I claim to have some little familiarity with the subject. I thought I had read all the books that it was possible to read upon it. I thought perhaps something had escaped my attention, and I was anxious to know what new authority my hon. friend could give to the House. But the only quotation which the hon. gentleman made was from Todd, a quotation with which we have been made familiar during the present session. If my hon. friend however will study Todd a little further, he will find that he has omitted from his speech the reference in which Todd applies directly to the case in hand. The question is, whether reports of this character are confidential or not. I have looked into the statutes to find what ought be the character of the reports which the heads of
departments should present to parliament. The language of the statute with regard to the Minister of Militia is the least satisfactory of all, because it simply says in section 126 of the Militia Act.
All regulations made under this Act, and an annual report of the state of the militia, shall be laid before parliament by the Minister of Militia and Defence within the first thirty days of the then next session thereof.
I intended to quote that : t forgot it.

I am very glad to be able to complete the speech of my hon. friend, but if he had quoted it, I suppose he would have sat down immediately, because there would he no further reason to go on with his speech. Since we agree on this point, let me read it again for the information of my hon. friend, and in order to refresh my own memory.
All regulations made under this Act and an annual report of the state of the militia shall be laid before parliament by the Minister of Militia and Defence.
The minister is hound to make a report upon the actual state of the militia, and nothing else. If he receives a plan from the Commander in Chief, or if he receives any proposed or suggested policy, there is no injunction on him to bring such before the House. The law says that his report must be confined strictly to what is the actual state of the militia. Let us see what information the other ministers are obliged to impart to the House. Section 6 of the Act with regard to the Department of the Interior says :
The Minister of the Interior shall annually lay before parliament within fifteen days after the meeting thereof, a report of the pro-cedings, transactions and affairs of the department, during the year then next preceding.
There also, the Minister of the Interior is enjoined ;-not to place before parliament what he contemplates ; not to place before parliament a statement as to what he may have in view for the future, but simply a statement of the transactions which have taken place during the year. Section i or the Act dealing with the Department ot Marine and Fisheries says :
The minister shall make and submit to the Governor General an annual report on all the works under his control, to be laid before both Houses of parliament within fifteen days from the commencement of each session, showing the state of each work, and the amount received and expended in respect thereof, with such further information as is requisite.
Here again the minister is enjoined only to acquaint parliament as to what he has done during the year. Section 6 of the Act dealing with the Secretary of State's De-. partment says :

The Secretarjr of State shall annually lay before parliament within ten days of the meeting thereof a report of the proceedings, transactions and affairs of the department during the year then next preceding.
Dealing with the Department of Inland Revenue, the Act says :
The Minister of Inland Revenue shall annually make to the Governor General, to be laid before parliament within fifteen days after the meeting thereof, a report and statement of the transactions and the affairs of the department during the year then next preceding.
Probably the most minute of all the departmental reports is that of the Post Office Department, and under the Act the Postmaster General is directed that he :
Shall annually make to the Governor General so that they may be laid before parliament within ten days after the meeting thereof, in each section the following reports which shall be made up to the 30th day of June then next preceding ; that is to say : general accounts current, what to contain and show :	payments for mail transport in detail ; salaries, &c., in detail ; incidental expenditure 'in detail ; cases of loss or abstraction of money leitters ; mioney order offices ; cost of money order system ; losses under money order system ; (lead letters ; posit office savings bank transactions, &c.
I have merely read the summarized side lines as to what is to be done by the Postmaster General under these different headings.
It will therefore be seen that the only injunction laid upon the heads of the different departments, is that they are directed to make a report for the information of parliament as to what has been the transactions of their departments for the past year. But, my hon. friend (Mr. Haggart) goes further and he says, that we should not only have information on what has been done, but that even the intentions ot the ministers, the policy which they contemplate, the views they may entertain, and the views and the policy as to which they may have been advised, should all be laid before parliament. Well, if the suggestion of my bon. friend were followed, it would be a great calamity in the management of the public affairs of this country. For instance, it would not be conducive to the best interest of the country to have the plans submitted to the Minister of Militia for the defence of the country, laid before parliament. I saw it stated somewhere recently, that parliament should be placed in possession of even the report prepared some years ago with regard to the defences of Canada. Of course, no one would pretend seriously that a secret report as to what ought be done for the defence of Canada should be made public. If that were done we might just as well give away the whole of our preparations in that direction. There Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
is no more reason why we should make public any plan suggested by the General Officer Commanding even if we did not approve of it. If such documents were made public, they would become the subject of wrangle between party and party-wrangle is not the proper word to use-hut they would become a matter of dispute and contention between parties bolding views on one side and the other. That would not be conducive to the best interests of Canada. It is far better that such a matter should be left between the minister and bis military
officer,	and that when a policy has been agreed upon then it should be discussed by parliament. If the policy suggested to the minister by his adviser should be made public so that it might become the bone of contention between contending parties, then in my opinion the value of our militia force would be greatly impaired. My hon. friend (Mr. Haggart) was good enough to state, that such documents as the reports of ambassadors from foreign courts should not be presented to parliament. I agree with him that the diplomatic reports from ambassadors at Paris, St. Petersburg, Berlin, Washington, or other foreign court, should be kept secret. The reason for that is obvious ? All the authorities agree that such reports should be kept secret, until such time has elapsed that they have no value except as a matter of history ; but so long as the question to which they relate are live issues, they must be kept sacredly guarded in the archives of the government to which they are addressed. If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Haggart) admits that diplomatic correspondence should be. kept secret, is not the reason at least just as strong, why military correspondence should be kept secret and sacred in the archives of the department to which it is addressed ?
My hon. friend stated otherwise, however. As to that, it is a matter of opinion which I have only to leave to the appreciation of the House. All the authorities-I need not repeat those which I gave to the House* the other day-are exactly contrary to the views entertained by my1 hon. friend. But my hon. friend went further to-day. He said that private letters should be laid on the table of the House and given to the public. Well, Sir, upon this point, let me for the information of my hon. friend, quote the standard book on this subject-' May on Parliamentary Practice.'
Returns may be moved for, either by order or address, relating to any public matters, in which the House or the Crown has jurisdiction. They may be obtained from all public
offices,	and from corporations, bodies, or officers constituted for public purposes, by Acts of parliament or otherwise ; but not from private associations, such as Lloyd's, for example, nor from individuals not exercising public functions. The papers and correspondence sought from government departments should be of a public and official. character,

and noit private or confidential. The opinions of the law officers of the Crown, given for the guidance of ministers, in any question of diplomacy or state policy, being included in the latter class, have generally been withheld from parliament.
If the opinions given by the law officers of the Crown for the guidance of the government have generally been withheld from parliament, and regarded as privileged and confidential, with What greater reason should not this same rule apply to the opinions of the military experts and advisers of the Crown ? May goes on to say :
In 1858, however, this rule was, under peculiar and exceptional circumstances, departed from, and the opinions of the law officers of the Crown, in regard to the case of the Cagliari, were laid before parliament. In 1871, in the select committee on the Thames Embank-dneut, a case submitted to the law officers being required, it was objected that the production of such a document was unusual ; but as it appeared that their opinion upon the case had already been laid before the House, the objection was withdrawn, and the case was produced before the committee.
But however ample the power of each House to enforce the production of papers, a sufficient cause must be shown for the exercise of that power ; and if considerations of public policy can be urged against a motion for papers, it is either withdrawn, or otherwise dealt with according to the judgment of the House.
That is to say, it should not be simply an arbitrary request for the gratification of an 'idle curiosity, or a curiosity of any kind; but a sufficient reason must be given to the House why the papers in the archives of the government should be given to the public, and the public interest must be shown.1 'My hon. friend has brought to the attention of the House such extraordinary theories to-day that I am not surprised that on minor points he should have erred as he has. If I understood the speech of my hon. friend aright, he has laid down the doctrine that under the law as it is to-day there are in the Militia Department two authorities, the civil authority and the military authority ; that the civil authority has certain functions to perform, and the military authority certain functions ; that the military authority is quite independent of the civil authority-that it is not dependent upon it. Well, I take the most complete issue with my hon. friend on this point. I say that the law of Canada to-day is the same as the law of England on this subject, that is, that the military authority is subject to tbe civil authority. The point is no longer debatable ; I will not for my part debate it, but will leave it to the judgment of the House. But I understand from the assent which was given to the words I used a moment ago that I have stated correctly the views of my hon. friend. I say I will not discuss that question. We are not
called on to-day, in the year 1904, to discuss a question like that before the Canadian people. The position of this government on that point was laid down more than three years ago-because this is not the first time we have had a disagreement with our military expert. In 1900, Colonel Prior, then a member of tbis House, put the following question in this House with regard to' the utterances of the gentleman who was then commander of the forces :
Has the attention of the government been called to the following words made use of by Major-General Hutton in a speech delivered by him at a farewell dinner tendered to him on the 14th Inst., by the officers of the Ottawa brigade :-
* I have used my utmost endeavour to create a national militia army worthy of the responsibilities which are peculiarly Its own, and which, to ensure success, must be placed upon a plane above all possibility of party political interference as regards its discipline, its personnel and its military machinery.
X should, however, feel more hopeful of the future of Canada if the government had even shown active interest in our recent efforts, for a higher efficiency, or indicated their approval of the principles upon which our efforts are based. I would ask you, however, in all due seriousness not to suppose that the severance of my ties with you is due to petty misunderstandings with the Minister of Militia upon minor issues of appointments or disciplinary matters, hut that it is due to broader, wider and vastly more important issues.'
Is it true that the government have not approved of the policy of the Major General Commanding, as set forth above ? Can the government inform this House what was the cause of the disagreement between them and the Major General ?
The answer I gave, speaking for the gov-' ernment, was as follows :
Ye,s, the attention of the government has been drawn to that portion of Major General Hutton's speech mentioned in the question, and to other portions also, equally reprehensible. There have been differences of opinion between the government and General Hutton. The government were disposed, now that he has been recalled for service in Africa, to let these differences pass without any comment. The government had reason to believe that this was in accordance with General Hutton's views, and therefore when the subject was brought up in the House a few days ago, the government refrained from making any statement on the subject. There is now no reason to follow that course any further. General Hutton in his speech has insinuated that his -differences with the government are due to a desire on the part of the latter to exercise improper political influence on the militia organization of the country. I desire, on the part of .the government, to say that there is absolutely no foundation for such a statement. The causes of difference between the government and General Hutton were not over any broad questions of general policy ; the causes of difference were that General Hutton was insubordinate and indiscreet, and deliberately ignored the authority of the minister

in the administration of the department. The government desire to state that while they will, at all times, be prepared to give the most careful consideration to any representations which may be unlade by the officer commanding the militia, it must be distinctly understood that any such officer, on accepting the position in question becomes from that time, an officer in the employment of and subject in all respects to the govenn'ment of Canada, and that he is to be regarded as the adviser, but not as entitled to control the Department of Militia. The government are responsible to the parliament and people of Canada for the due administration of each and every branch of the public service, and they would be derelict to their duty if they were to permit any subordinate official, under any circumstances, to take upon himself to disregard the instructions he may receive from the constitutional head of his department.
I have nothing- to add to what was stated on that occasion by me as the head of the government. This was the position we took, and this is the position by which we are to be judged by this House and this country.	.

Mr. Speaker, the right hon. gentleman has Introduced a subject which those supporting the government are very anxious to introduce on occasions of this kind. That is the question of the subordination of the military to the civil power in this country. That is not,' the question which is before the House, but as my right hon. friend has said a few words about it, I shall do likewise. There is no doubt under the statute as to who is responsible to parliament for the administration of the militia:
There shall be a Minister of Militia and Defence who shall he charged with and responsible for the administration of the militia force, including all matters involving expenditure and, of fortifications, gunboats, ordnance, arms, armouries, stores, munitions and habiliments of war belonging to Canada.
AVhen the Prime Minister undertakes to argue that that statute means what he says, he is simply setting up a man of straw which no one but (himself has any regard for. The argument of toy hon. friend~for I a nark (Mr. Haggart) was this. He argued mat in this country, owing to the difference in legislation, the Commander in Chief has certain larger powers than those he possesses in Great Britain at present, but he never argued that the Commander in Chief wu>
rot subordinate to the Minister oif Militia in this sense, that the Minister of Militia is ultimately responsible to parliament and the country. There is no use in arguing a matter which is not in controversy and which is simply introduced for the purpose of taking away the attention of the public from that which is really in question. But let us remember that although the Minister of Militia is ultimately responsible and that the Commander in | Sir WILFRID LAURIER
Chief holds his position under the government of this country, the latter officer has under the statute certain responsibilities as well. And they are these :
1.	The General Officer Commanding is charged by statute, under the orders of Her Majesty, with the military command and discipline of the militia.
2.	He is the principal adviser of the Minister of Militia and Defence on all military questions ; - Is charged with the general supervision of the military branch of the department ; issues general orders ; and holds periodical inspections of the militia.
3.	He is charged with the distribution, quartering, and localization of the militia ; with the preparation and maintenance of detailed plans for mobilization ; with .the preparation of schemes for offensive and defensive operations ; and with the collection and compilation of military information.
4.	He recommends- to the Minister of Militia and Defence fit and proper persons for appointment to commissions in the militia ; and proposes fit and proper officers for promotion, for staff and other military appointments, and for military honours and rewards.
5.	He is charged with the military education and training of the officers, non-commissioned officers and men of the active militia, including the supervision of the Royal Military College of Canada, and the several Royal Schools of Military Instruction throughout the Dominion.
He Is charged witli these things because parliament has seen fit to entrust them to trim by that which is equivalent to an Act of parliament; and when the right hon. gentleman says that the General Officer Commanding is to be a mere automaton and' is not to have the power of thinking for himself or of having any policy with regard to military affairs, he takes a position which cannot be supported by any one who is capable of understanding the language I have just read and bestows upon it one moment's thought or reflection. Is it pretended for one moment that the Minister of Militia is an expert in military affairs ? Is it not often the case that the gentleman filling the political position of Minister of Militia is absolutely unacquainted with military affairs ? Is such a gentleman to judge of all tfiese things, and is the General Officer Commanding, invested with all these powers, responsible under the statute, to be a man without a policy, without the power to recommend ? And if he does have the temerity to recommend, is the political officer above him to be at liberty to use his own discretion in suppressing the report ? The Prime Minister takes the position that he is, and if I am doing him an injustice in that regard, will he be good enough to correct me 1
Let me now deal with the question of this report which has been furnished to the House. But before doing so let me remark On at certain newspapers in this country, which are supposed to be absolutely in the

confidence of the government, profess to have a remarkable acquaintance with the contents of that report. I do not know whether that has shocked my right hon. friend. He has been sometimes shocked at revelations of that kind in the House, but I have not observed him to manifest any indignation at the fact that a document of that kind, which is not proper to be submitted to parliament, is considered apparently proper to submit to his political friends outside the House. How is it that this was done ? Was it for the purpose of discrediting Lord Dundonald by conveying to the public what I venture to think will be found a misleading statement of his report, while at the same time denying to Lord Dundonald the right to put himself properly before the country by the production of that report, as he handed it in in the first instance ? I ask that question because it is a question that naturally occurs to one, under the very peculiar circumstances of the present time, when a ministry declines to place a document on the table of the House and allows their organs throughout the country to inform the people of its contents. This document, according to the Prime Minister, should be suppressed. It seems to me his argument went a little too far. Does my hon. friend take the position that every one of these reports to which he has referred to-day, including the report of the Department of Militia and Defence, could be suppressed by the minister in charge of the department, and that that minister would discharge his duty under the law to the House and the country by simply saying : I have had reports of the officers of my department, but in my discretion I did not see fit to publish them, and place them upon the table of the House as the report of his department ? My hon. friend says that the Minister of Militia was justified in withholding this report and for this reason. He referred to section 126 of the Militia Act, -which says :
All regulations made under this Act and the annual report of the state of the militia shall be laid before parliament by the Minister of Militia and Defence.
Who is to give the Minister of Militia that report upon the state of the militia? Who is his proper adviser under the statute ? I have read the statute which says that the General Officer Commanding is the proper adviser of the Minister of Militia and that he is charged wit!h the conduct and discipline of the militia._Then if the Minister of
Militia is to give a report to parliament upon the state of the militia, upon whose advice must he act, and whose report must he receive? He must receive and publish to parliament and the country the report of the General Officer Commanding. But my rigfit hon. friend ventures to say that this report of Lord Dundonald was not a
report on the state of the militia. Am I correct in that ?
I think the report of Lord Dundonald, so far as it went, as regards the state of the militia, was published. It was as regards his policy, that it was not published.

I would like to have something more than tthe thought of my right bon. friend. I would like to have an absolute statement. He has founded an argument upon it. He said that the Minister of Militia had a right to suppress this report because it did not come within the terms of this statute. That is what I understood him to say, if he said anything. Does he adhere to that?

If my hon. friend (Mr. R. L. Borden) cannot understand what I say, I am sorry for it. I stated that the Minister of Militia had put in his report that part of the document prepared by the General Officer Commanding which related to the state of the militia, but he refused to publish the part which suggested a policy.

I will try to understand my right hon. friend. That portion of the report which dealt with the state of the militia has been jjublished and that part which dealt with the policy and a scheme of the defence has not been published.
I understand so.

Lord Dundonald does not so understand it and there is a direct issue between him and the government ip that regard. I will read from Lord Dundonald's statement :
One extremely serious case of interference was the suppression of the important parts of my first annual report on the militia. After studying the situation with great care, I came to certain conclusions and thought out a certain plan. For convenience of reference I divided my report for the year 1902 into two halves. Part, I. was a simple diary of events. Part II. contained my description of the condition of the militia and an outline of a comprehensive scheme for reorganizing the force upon lines suitable to the country.
It contained, it will be observed, a comprehensive description of the condition of the militia. Now, the statute prescribes the minister to place before parliament annually a report of the state of the militia. And it appears from the statement of Lord Dundonald that that which the minister is required to place before parliament was placed in his hands by Lord Dundonald. Yet, the government, for some reason best known to themselves have seen fit to suppress it. There have been a great many reasons given for the suppression of this report. I have just dealt for a moment with one of them. And does not my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and do not hon. gentlemen in

this House think that there was some reason for receiving a report from the principal adviser of the government in that regard, when an hon. gentleman on the other side of the House, an expert in military affairs, the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. A. T. Thomson) from his place in this House, last year described, in terms, I will venture to say, more scathing than any than Lord Dundonald had used, the condition of the militia in Canada. He said that the militia called out for annual training were intended to be a skeleton, but that from that they had diminished to a skeleton of a skeleton and now they had to come down to the condition where they could only be described as the shadow of a skeleton of a skeleton. When this is the condition, and when we have a report of the General Officer Commanding suppressed, and when we find that gentleman stating, as a man who has occupied high rank in the army and who has held a high position in Canada, that this report contained a .description of the militia in Canada, and when we find that that very report required by law to be published] is in fact suppressed, is there not some room, in the view of my right hon. friend for criticism in this House and in the country concerning the action of the government in that regard. Another reason advanced for the suppression of this document was that put forward by the Minister of Militia the other day-that the part- suppressed had been marked ' private.' He intended to state by that remark,-as he explained later on, that it was inclosed in a letter marked ' private.' And it eventually transpired that, so far from the report being marked ' private,' Lord Dundonald did not so mark it and expressly desired that it should be published. The Minister of Militia made the argument, as he is entitled to do, if it is worth anything, that because this part of the report was included in a letter marked ' private ' he was not at liberty to publish it. But, so far as that is concerned, he had Lord Dundonald's permission to publish it, even Lord Dundonald's request to publish it. And, further than that this very curious aspect of the matter is presented that the part of the report that was published was inclosed in the same letter as the other. So that if the reason given by the minister was a good one, then, according to his own argument he has committed a breach of confidence by publishing part I of that report. If this report described the condition of the militia as unsatisfactory in some respects, it might be inconvenient for the government to publish it. But is it not a proper thing that matters of this kind should be brought to the attention of parliament ? As I have already said, can every report put in by a deputy head of a department be suppressed or set aside by the government simply for the reason that it may happen to contain something that is regarded as not advantageous, politically, to the Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
gentlemen who happen to sit on the treasury benches. Suppose the Auditor General's Report contained something not exactly gratifying to the administration, would it be a proper thing for the administration to say that the suppression of publication of that report was a matter absolutely within their discretion ? My right hon. friend referred to matters that are absolutely distinct, and yet, in his argument he has mixed those two things together. There is no doubt that there are documents which may properly be withheld from parliament. And with respect to these documents hon. gentlemen, whether on the government side or on the opposition side must always entrust a certain discretion to the government, must trust the good faith of the government in declaring to the House or parliament as a whole that reasons of public policy make it necesssary that information should be withheld for the present. That is the position that I am prepared to stand by as absolutely as my right hon. friend. But it is another thing for the government to arrogate to themselves the right, when they are not able to place before the House any reasons of public policy, to withhold from parliament documents such as those mentioned by my hon. friend from South Lanark (Mr. Haggart) to-day-for instance, a report prescribed by statute and conveying certain information, or a petition addressed to the Prime Minister praying the government to grant aid for an enterprise to be undertaken by a private corporation. These are not to be withheld from parliament, because there is no consideration of public policy which demands that they should be so withheld. Therefore, I say that, so far as the argument is concerned, the right hon. gentleman has based his argument not upon the considerations which apply to that, but absolutely on other matters and on other considerations. Then, we have the statement of Lord Dundonald that a portion of another report was suppressed, that portions of it were eliminated. I would like to ask my right hon. friend whether he thinks that the report of another officer, or any other document should be laid before this House in a mutilated condition without making it known to the House that certain portions of it had been eliminated ? For example, is it the proper thing for the Minister of Inland Revenue to eliminate from the reports of his officers certain portions of those reports and then bring down these documents as if they were complete. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) took the ground-and it is one with which I would not coincide-in regard to a matter already debated in this House, that if documents of an official character were in possession of the government, the government were justified in denying that those documents existed. They are not justified in denying that they exist, but they are justified in stating that they exist

and also in stating their reasons of public policy why the documents are not brought down or brought down only in part. That is the course followed in the mother country. That is the course the government of this country followed in regard to the documents relating to the Alaska Boundary question. Because in that case we had it indicated py stars, in despatch after despatch, that certain portions were regarded as confidential and were therefore eliminated from the despatches as a whole.
That is the course which should have been pursued in regard to this report, if any portion of it was eliminated. Of course, if the General Officer Commanding took the report back and altered it himself that would not apply, but the General Officer Commanding states, whether rightly or wrongly I do not know, that not only did he do that, not only did he modify the report in accordance with the wishes of the Minister of Militia, but that after he had done that, whole paragraphs, and even whole pages, were withdrawn from the report without consultation with him, and the report, to the best of my knowledge, was brought down without stating those omissions.
My hon. friend from Lanark (Mr. Hag-gart) dealt with some other documents, about one or two of which I desire to say a word. He referred to what is known as the Blair memorandum. When Mr. Blair placed his resignation in the hands of His Excellency, and when the Prime Minister and Mr. Blair came down to make their explanations in parliament, I think, not merely in courtesy to the House, but in fairness to the House, that the full reasons for Mr. Blair's lesignation should have been placed before the House. I took the opportunity of asking the Prime Minister several weeks ago whether or not there was any correspondence between this government and Mr. Blair other than that which was disclosed to this House at the time these explanations were given. My right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) on that occasion said that he did not know of any other correspondence, but would make inquiries and would inform me, but from that time up to the present I have not had the pleasure of receiving any intimation from the right hon. gentleman on that point, and I am inclined to think the letters themselves which have been brought down contain certain intrinsic evidences that they are not the only correspondence which took place between Mr. Blair and the government on that occasion. Let me say that it would have been a proper thing on that occasion for the Prime Minister to have informed the House, even if Mr. Blair did not see fit to do so, that the difficulty between Mr. Blair and the government was not only with regard to Mr. 31air's opposition to the policy proposed by the government, but was also due to the fact that Mr. Blair himself thought it necessary that the proposed National Transcon 184
tinental Railway should be built as a government undertaking. The document, to which reference has been made, set out Mr. Blair's views on that most fully. I concede at once that while that matter was being debated in Council the government were perfectly justified in holding that document from the country. It is not for the government, when matters are being discussed in Council, to disclose differences in the cabinet, differences which must always arise in any government and which must be settled as best they may. But when these differences have culminated in the resignation of a minister, and when the government and the minister resigning purport to convey to the House and the country the reasons for his resignation, I submit to my right hon. friend in all fairness that they were not treating the House and the country properly or in a constitutional way in stating to the House and the country only a portion of the reasons for that resignation and in withholding one of the principal reasons on account of which that resignation has taken place. There was no difficulty about bringing down Mr. Blair's memorandum. The formality of asking the Governor General might have been necessary, but that formality was just as easy with regard to this so-called memorandum as with regard to the letters which were produced and the explanations which were made in this House, and I venture to say, in terms of as mild criticism as I can use, that the government seem to me to have acted in a disingenuous way in withholding that document at the time when these explanations were made.
I shall not take up much time in reference to the Grand Trunk Pacific petition, which, as my right hon. friend has said, has already been dealt with in a previous debate. Let me, however, make just four statements with regard to it First, it related to a public matter ; secondly, it petitioned for public aid; thirdly, it was acted on ; and fourthly, it was obviously disclosed to a gentleman who was put up to answer Mr. Blair in the debate on the Grand Trunk Pacific. There can be no doubt about that. My right hon. friend has stated in this House that he did not disclose that petition to the hon. member for North Norfolk. I stated then, and I state now, that I accept his assurance in that regard, but I tell him that if he wishes me to believe that some member of his cabinet did not disclose that document to the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. -Charlton), if he wishes me to believe that the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) was not made acquainted with the terms of that petition, then he asks me to believe something which my understanding absolutely forbids me to believe, because it is impossible that the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton), speaking as he did on this subject, could have quoted elaborately and exactly



5S00
the very terms of that document, if he had not been made acquainted with them at the time. We must not forget that this was a gentleman put up to speak as the government expert, pronounced by the Prime Minister to be the greatest authority on transportation in this parliament, and let me say that if that document was submitted to the hon. member for North Norfolk, however confidential it might have been in the first instance, the government, so long as it proposed to follow ordinary constitutional usage, was absolutely bound to place in the possession of every member of this House just as much Information on that subject as was in the possession of the hon. member for North Norfolk. Otherwise, the government was treating this parliament with contempt, and did treat this parliament with contempt when it placed in the possession of that hon. gentleman, who was speaking for this government in that regard, information which they did not see fit to disclose to this House until at the end of a very long debate this year the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) saw fit, for party purposes, and for party purposes alone, to read the whole document to this House. That is the constitutional usage with regard to it; and I am studiously avoiding any language that could possibly be regarded as too severe ; I want to speak moderately, and to deal with the matter in the light of what I regard as the proper constitutional usage.
Let me here advert to another matter. A practice which is becoming very common with this government, the practice, while parliament is In session, of communicating to the public press, days before communication is made to parliament, documents respecting matters that have been discussed in parliament and that are of the greatest possible public interest. I stand as strongly as any one in this House for giving to the press the earliest possible information with regard to public matters, but I say it is a contempt of parliament to do as this government has repeatedly done, to give information to the government organs of this country, and to allow day after day to pass withholding that information from parliament, although it ought to be of the greatest possible interest to those who sit in this House. I refer to the matter of the Tread-gold concession as an instance. My right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) will remember that we spent one or two days last year discussing that matter. We on this side contended that that concession should have been repealed, that it was an improper concession. A commission was eventually appointed, although its scope was not as full as we thought it should have been, yet when the government, acting upon some intimation from the commission, upon some information at least, first communicated to the organs of the government the fact that they had taken action, and had not even the courtesy to lay upon the table of this Ml. R. L. BORDEN.
House a copy of the Order in Council cancelling this concession. The information that the government has so acted is communicated to the organs of the government, and the government has not even the courtesy to lay upon the table of this House a copy of the Order in Council. I do not think that is treating parliament with proper courtesy.

I must say to my hon. friend that in So_far as his criticism goes, if his statement were a fact, I would agree with him altogether. Very often, I am sorry to say, information goes to the press and it is impossible to say how it goes to the press. In reference to this matter I saw in the press that this Order in Council had been cancelled but I cannot trace it up to any source. I may say, however, that it does not come from any authorized source.

I accept the assurance of my right, hon. friend. I naturally supposed that as this had been published the intimation had been given to the press by the government. My remarks in so far as that is concerned have no application in view of the right hon. gentleman's statement. But I may say here that if I searched my memory carefully I could find other occasions when the fault to which I have just adverted has been committed, by the government. There is just one other matter to which I wish to refer in connection with public documents and that is to the letters of Colonel Whitley to the hon. Minister of Agriculture. I suggested the other day that Colonel Whitley's request that these letters should be regarded as confidential might have been instigated by the Minister of Agriculture. The Minister of Agriculture has not contradicted that suggestion, I have every reason to believe that if Colonel Whitley did make that request to the hon. Minister of Agriculture there was the previous request of the hon. minister to Colonel Whit-' ley that such communications should be made to him. But what had Colonel Whitley to do with it after all ? Is not Colonel Whitley an officer of this government, paid by this country for the discharge of the duty which involved the writing of those letters and are those letters to be withheld from parliament simply because it suits the convenience of the hon. Minister of Agriculture and of Colonel Whitley to have them so withheld ? They are from a subordinate officer of the government to the Minister of Agriculture who claims the right to Act as a public man, as a minister of the Crown in reference to a public matter. In what respect can they be confidential ? They relate to the appointment of officers in the regiment referred to. Further than that my hon. friend from South Lanark (Mr. Hag-gart) produces an argument which was made only the other day in the House by the

hon. Minister of Militia and Defence (Sir Frederick Borden). He states what is very true that these letters are referred to in the letter brought down. .One of the arguments of the hon. Minister of Militia the other day was that he had the right to ask Lord Dundonald to withdraw certain paragraphs from his report because those paragraphs related to documents not brought down, and he said to Lord Dundonald that if the report containing these allusions is placed before the House then the House will have absolute right to call for these documents. If that is a good argument in the mouth of the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence, is it not a good argument in the mouth of any other hon. gentleman in this House ? There are letters brought down containing an allusion to the letters from Colonel Whitley and if the argument of the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence, supported as it was to-day by the argument of my hon. friend from South Lanark, is correct then the production of these letters is in itself the best justification' why this House can call for the documents referred to in tihese letters. Yet they are withheld from this Houes upon the mere pretense that they can be confidential.
Mr. Speaker, some reference has been made to-day by those who have spoken to the subordination of the military power to the civil power in this country and in fact the line of argument which is taken in a certain portion of the press has been followed, namely, that there was some attempt on the part of Lord Dundonald to impose what is called militarism on this country. That is the red herring 'if X may term it so. Let me say that I have found no evidence in any document that has been published or in any communication that has been made that - shows Lord Dundonald in any such light. I am not dealing now with the question of his alleged insubordination at the banquet. If the argument which my right hon. friend the Prime Minister made a day or two ago were correct,-I do not think it is correct-every officer at the Dominion Rifle meeting this year for example who spoke in terms of commendation of the hon. Minister of Militia would be liable to immediate dismissal for so doing. That is what the argument of my hon. friend leads to. He quoted the regulation which only has reference to military discipline and to military officers and he applied that to the relations existing between the General Officer Commanding and the Minister of Militia and Defence. That regulation makes it just as much an offence for any officer to refer to his superior officer in terms of commendation as in terms of disapprobation ; therefore, hundreds of officers all over this country who have spoken flatteringly of the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence will be subject to dismissal if my right hon. friend's argument be correct. But,
IS It
there is nothing in it. Those gentlemen were perfectly proper in uttering their commendations. They were not violating any military rule or regulation which had any application to the case. Indeed my right hon. friend has extended his argument a little farther than what I was suggesting, because his argument, if it means anything, means that the hon. Minister of Agriculture is the military superior officer of the General Officer Commanding and that the General Officer Commanding by reason of referring to the Minister of Agriculture is guilty of a breach of discipline toward his military superior officer and for that reason may be disciplined and dismissed. Well, 1 think that the argument need only be stated to refute itself and I will not deal further with it.
Lord Dundonald, as I understand it, has never sought to place the military power over the civil power. What he has sought to do is to prevent the interposition of the hon. Minister of Agriculture between himself and his subordinate officers and in doing that he is upholding the civil power itself, because it is the civil power of this country exercised through parliament which has declared that Lord Dundonald shall have certain duties and that his subordinate officers shall have certain duties. If the hon. Minister of Agriculture interferes with these subordinate officers in the performance of their duty it is he who is guilty of violating the constitutional rights of the people, and when Lord Dundonald protested against that interference of the hon. Minister of Agriculture it was Lord Dundonald who upheld the constitutional rights of the people of this country. My right hon. friend has been somewhat sensitive about the criticism made upon certain words which he used in this House in speaking them. I did not think them worth upon this subject. I have never alluded to alluding to and I was ready then as I am ready on all occasions to accept the right hon. gentleman's statement as to the word he intended to use and the manner in which he intended to use it. This is a courtesy which we owe to each other according to the rules of the House. But, my right hon. friend must not forget perhaps that he is not always so ready to extend a courtesy of that kind to hon. gentlemen on this side of the House. When I stood up in my place during this session and stated that a certain word, reported by ' Hansard ' as having been used by me, had not been used by me and gave my word to the House as the fact, did I find my right hon. friend accepting that statement ?
No. I did not. I found my right hon. friend speaking in-well, in language that might be regarded as meaning that he was rather doubtful-in rather a discourteous way with regard to the incident ; so that I was compelled to write a letter to the chief of the

* Hansard ' staff, and to produce evidence from the original notes of the shorthand writer in support of that word of mine which I thought might be accepted by my right hon. friend. Let not my right hon. friend be too sensitive unless he is prepared to be uniformly courteous himself. I said not one word about the expression which he used the other day. I do not propose to say anything about it except to make the allusion which I am now making. The right hon. gentleman must remember that he told us that he is not at all sensitive to criticism, when I called him in question for some words which he had used with regard to the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Osier). He practically said then :	I will use any
language I see fit, and I will not shrink from criticism. But at the first breath of any strong criticism we find my right hon. friend a little excited, and we find him using very strong and very-well, very militant language towards those who may venture to criticise him. My right hon. friend has a perfect right to use any language he sees fit within the rules of this House, and others in the House and without the House have also the right to use such moderate criticism with regard to his language as they may deem proper. The right hon. gentleman referred only the other day to a great many illustrations of the use of the words ' stranger ' and ' foreigner, ' and indeed in speaking on the subject he said that he regarded Lord Dundonald as a stranger only to the eastern townships. It was only necessary to remind the House that Lord Dundonald was not himself doing this work in the eastern townships ; it was the officers under Lord Dundonald who were doing the wrork there and they should have been left uninterfered with by the Minister of Agriculture. Lord Dundonald himself was not going to the eastern townships to make a selection of officers ; he left that as the law directed to the officers whose duty it was to perform that service. I do not for one moment question my right hon. friend's assurance as to the sense in which he intended these words, and I for my part am always ready on this or any other occasion to accept his assurance on such a matter. Let me however quote to him, from that well of pure and undefilecf English, a few words which may be of service in interpreting what the ordinary sense of such words is : .
Now, therefore, ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens with the saints. -'Ephesians II., 19.
That is perhaps a pretty good illustration in which the three expressions ' strangers, ' and * foreigners ' and * fellow citizens ' may be used. I am willing to accept the right hon. gentleman's assurance that he meant no suggestion to the contrary, but I do declare that notwithstanding any assurance to the contrary from any quarter, a man of the race and the birth of the Earl of Dun-Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
donald will always be regarded in Canada, not as a foreigner or a stranger, but as a fellow-citizen.

speechtext: This estimate includes the salaries, rent and expenses of the new agency recently established in Montreal. It is proposed to increase the salaries of the agents in British Columbia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. The salary of the British Columbia agent is to be increased from 81,600 to $1,800. The agent, in addition to his ordinary duties, performs the duties of inspector of lighthouses and examines masters and mates for certificates, for which he is allowed $200 a year. The St. John agent receives $1,600, while his predecessor received $2,000 ; and it is proposed to increase his salary to $1,800. In Nova Scotia the agent's salary is $1,600. He is provided with a staff of assistants, and it is not proposed to increase his salary. The agent in Prince Edward Island receives $1,400. Besides his duty as agent, he inspects all the lighthouses. In Quebec the agent's salary is $2,200 a year, and he has a competent and efficient staff to assit him.
How many agencies are there altogether ?
One in Quebec, one in New Brunswick, one in Nova Scotia, one in Prince Edward Island, one in British Columbia, and a sub-marine agency at Montreal, established a year ago.
What amounts are paid for rent ?
I am informed that they are all government properties except the Montreal office, which is rented from a private estate and the rent is $2,000.
Has the same rent been paid for some years ?

In Montreal it is a new agency which was established a year ago, but wTe have aggregated into that office the pilots, the cabin space inspectors and the steamboat inspectors.

Inspection of lighthouses and aids to navigation, $502,000.

speechtext:
The extensive improvements authorized in the lighting of the Upper St. Lawrence, comprises the introduction of compressed acetylene instead of oil in lighthouses, and the use of acetylene for the buoy service instead of oil or Pintsch gas, and also the use, as far as possible, of range lights instead of single lights and gas buoys. The rearrangement of the existing system of lights will be considered as soon as possible by the lighthouse board which has been established. Last session, an estimate was given of the cost of converting the lighting of the river, and the apparatus needed procured from the Safety
Car Heating and Lighting Company, of New York, as it was not made in Canada. Also provision was made for a suitable buoy depot at a central point on the river, between Dickinson's Landing and Prescott, where there should be ample store room space, dock room for steamers, and land for storage gas, can and spar buoys. The selection of a suitable depot was made at Prescott, and the department obtained an option on the property owned by John La-batt, of London, Ont. The price paid for the property including wharfs, buildings and land, $26,500. This location is an ideal place for a buoy depot, is centrally situated and will be the headquarters for assembling apparatus for the lighthouse service of the Dominion, and provision is being made for the manufacture of apparatus now purchased abroad. $35,000 was the sum estimated for the depot, but the department was able to make the purchase for $26,500. Last year $80,000 was placed in the estimates to provide for the construction of a lightship to be placed on Lurcher Shoal at the entrance of the Bay of Fundy. It was also found necessary in the interests of navigation that a lightship should be placed at the East Point of Anticosti. A contract was entered into with the Poison Iron Works of Toronto, to construct the two lightships for the sum of $179,500. I may say that- at the time this amount of $502,000 was placed in the estimates, being the same amount as voted last year, the department had not at that time completed its policy in respect to aids to navigation for the next fiscal year. The lighthouse board is now passing upon a number of applications before the department which have been held over awaiting the organization of the board. These will comprise new lighthouses, fog alarms and buoys, but until the board completes its labours, it will not be possible to give an estimate of the amount that will be required for these new aids. The amount required for these aids together with the balance mentioned above, will appear in the supplementary estimates. The fog alarms of the Dominion comprise a very important class of aids to navigation and those in the St. Lawrence are especially important in view of the increase in number and tonnage of the ships utilizing the route. Provision will be made for the installation of the best machinery obtaiuable which will make the system second to none. The cost is estimated at $175,000. Complaints .have been made in the past about the lighting of the St. Lawrence route, and the estimates provide for a sum of $50,000 which will be sufficient to install the most modern apparatus that can be obtained. When the improvements provided by this vote are carried out no further complaints should be made concerning the lighting of this important trade artery. As indicated above, the department had purchased a depot at Prescott, which will be utilized for the as-

sembly and manufacture of lighthouse apparatus for the Dominion. It is necessary that a basin should be provided for the government steamers, and that a machine shop should be erected for the manufacture of certain classes of apparatus not made in Canada. This will keep the larger proportion of the vote for this purpose within the country. The sum of $60,000 is required for this purpose, many of the lights in the lighthouses of the Dominion are neither powerful enough nor are their lights sufficiently charateristic, and it is necessary to take steps to remedy this state of affairs. This will be done by the substitution of gas for oil as the illuminant, thereby increasing the power of the lights and also permitting them to be made more characteristic. The sum of $100,000 is asked for this purpose, and it is estimated that it "'ill provide for the conversion of about 300 lighthouses. The apparatus will be designed by the engineers of the department. The extension of the gas buoy system in the Quebec, Nova Scotia and Georgian Bay districts calls for the erection of three gas pumping stations. These will be located at Quebec, Halifax and Parry Sound, respectively. $50,000 was asked for this purpose. It is desirable to continue the lighting of the channel from Quebec to Sore], which was commenced last year by the opening up of the Sorel-Montreal division, and which permitted night navigation between these two points. The arrangement has been of great benefit to the shipping interests, and has been appreciated by them. I may say, as regards the inauguration of the new lights between Montreal and Sore], that they have been so successful that steamers have been able to leave Montreal during the night and navigate the whole distance of forty-five miles with perfect safety.

The article dated January 15, 1904, and is as follows :
Canada has gone ahead very rapidly during the past year, and Montreal, as the export centre of the Dominion, has unquestionably had its full share of the enhanced activity. In the ' Annual Review ' which is issued by the Montreal ' Gazette,' it is stated that in the great staple products, the export business from Montreal during the season of navigation was larger than from any other port on the American continent, not excepting New York. ' No stronger evidence,' it is argued, ' of the cheapness, convenience, and advantage of the St. Lawrence route than this fact affords could well he given, nor can the end of the period of prosperity be yet discerned.' Notwithstanding, the year was not considered to be quite satisfactory, by shipping men, and high rates of insurance on cargoes and hulls are mentioned as one of the causes. We are told, however, that it is possible to attach too much importance to this matter, and that, if insurance is the drawback it is represented to be, it is surprising that the established lines increase the traffic and that new ones spring up to compete with them. The real difficulty, it is suggested, is that keen competition has reduced the rates at Amercian ports to an abnormally low figure. On the other hand, it is frankly acknowledged that when freights are low the insurance question becomes of greater consequence. It would appear that the accidents on the St. "Lawrence route were slightly heavier in 1903 than in the preceding year. Among the most serious were the total wreck of the ' Monterey,' and the disasters to
the 'Norwegian' and the 'Manchester Trader.' But it is put forward that these accidents can hardly he ascribed to the danger of the route, since they have all been proved to be due to error in judgment or incompetency on the part of the navigators. That is, perhaps, putting it rather high. No doubt carelessness has played a rather prominent part in certain St. Lawrence disasters, but insurance rates to a certain extent speak for themselves. Human judgment is probably no more fallible in the St. Lawrence than elsewhere, but aids to human judgment may possibly be numerous or less effective than in some other waters. Casualty, how-ever, has happily not prevented Montreal's shipping from forging ahead. The total number of boats which arrived in the port was 797 last year, as against 758 in 1902.
