Not in the light of day, but in the light of the illumination, I should say, that the hon. gentleman has been endeavouring to spread over the St. Lawrence for the purpose of protecting the lives and property of the people of Canada. Yet, in face of this occurrence, we are told that we have to wait some four or five years more before we will be able to escape catas-trophies of that kind. But I desire to speak seriously upon this matter. I hope the hon. gentleman is not going to spend all his money in the upper St. Lawrence, between Montreal and Sorel, because there are other parts of the country that are entitled Mr. FOWLER.
to receive some little consideration from the hon. gentleman. I am not going to ask very much of him, but I hope he will grant the little I do ask, and I trust at the same time that he will extend beyond even -what I ask and give his careful attention to the regions to the west of Montreal, because there must be many parts of the country where lighthouses will be required. I believe that on the upper lakes, Lake Superior especially, he will find ample opportunity for spending money and improving the system to assist the enormous amount of navigation that is coursing through those waters. I presume the hon. minister has visited the St. Clair river at some time in his life. If lie has not visited Sarnia within the last five or ten years, I would counsel him to pay a flying visit to that district and to sit down for about half an hour and watch the number of vessels which pass during that time. I am* quite sure he would be astonished. I have heard it said that on that river, and I have not the slightest doubt but what it is quite true, there are more vessels passing through than there are practically crossing the Atlantic ocean. There is an enormous amount of navigation on the upper lakes and rivers, and yet it seems that all these waters are to be neglected for the sake of the improvement of the St. Lawrence river. I draw the hon. minister's attention to the fact that the navigation of the St. Lawrence is a mere trifle. It is a very small thing compared with the navigation of the upper lakes and the rivers connecting these lakes. I do not suppose it amounts to a tenth part- perhaps I may not be far astray when I say the twentieth part-of the navigation of these inland waters, and surely the hon. gentleman will be able to spare some of this $500,000 to give some attention to the lighting up of the rivers and lakes west of Montreal. But the particular item to which I desire to draw the attention of the hon. minister is one in which I am rather personally interested, and I think I need only mention it to bring it to the recollection of the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries.
I say Minister of Marine and Fisheries, because the matter I refer to has more reference to fisheries than to marine. One year ago, after the hon. gentleman came into office, I drew his attention to the case in my own county of the little town of Bronte, where the government had been constructing a wharf and dredging out the mouth of the creek for the purpose of improving the harbour. I desire to remind him that in that neighbourhood, in Lake Ontario, adjacent to the town of Bronte, a very considerable amount of fishing is going on. It is the home of the Cisco herring. The fishery extends out ten or fifteen miles, and a very large amount of fishing is being done. Very frequently, in the late autumn, storms blow up on the lake and the fishermen, as on the Atlantic coast, are subjected to very great danger. Sometimes the men are caught out

in a storm while setting or taking in their nets, and on a dark night it is difficult for them to find their way back to port. I have asked the minister-and I am sorry to say that no action has been taken-if he could not take, say, $200 or $300-I do not think it would cost more than $200-to erect a skeleton lighthouse sufficiently high to place a light that will be seen for ten or fifteen miles out by the fishermen on a dark night. It need only be lighted for a comparatively small portion of the year, but it would be a guide to the fishermen in the darkness to a port of safety, and perhaps be the means of saving valuable lives. The expenditure would be small compared with the advantages that would be gained, and I am quite sure that the minister would not only confer a favour on these people, but that he would receive their hearty approbation and thanks if he would not allow this matter to drift along year after year, but if he would put somebody to work on this small job, and during the current summer, before the rough weather of the fall sets in, have a light erected there in order to give to these people the advantage which I have suggested.
I presume the minister will tell me that he does not want to erect a lighthouse until the pier is built. I think I can remove that difficulty. The minister can erect a light at the end of the pier so far as it has been completed, and if that be found an unsuitable location, and I do not think it will, it can be changed afterwards to the end of the pier when completed. Heretofore lights' have been built upon the bank of the lake or the people have placed lights in their window's hoping that the fishermen would see them, so that I am sure a lighthouse erected at the present end of the pier would be an improvement. The construction of this wharf seems to be one of these interminable jobs that have a beginning and never have an end. It has been going on for four years, whereas if ordinary business sense had been applied the whole work including the lighthouse would have been constructed in one or two seasons, so that in the dark and stormy nights of the fall, the fishermen would be able to return thanks to him for the consideration shown for their welfare by providing this necessary essential to their operations. I appeal to the minister to be good enough to give this matter his immediate attention, and if he does I am sure it will be appreciated in that section of the country.

Chief engineer.

Special officers are appointed to look after the buoys and keep them in place, and they are pati-olling the St. Lawrence all the time. Sometimes it happens that a buoy gets out of place. It may be dragged by a boat that may have sfranded near the buoy. As soon as this

is brought to the notice of the official in
charge, if he is not himself on the spot,' it is remedied. Such things will happen, and cannot be prevented. I would like to ask the minister what power he exercises with regard to the southern points of Newfoundland.	'

We have no power, i All we can do in these foreign waters is draw the attention of the Home government to anything that is wrong. What is the result of the investigation which the minister made on the coast of the United States ?

At present we are installing four stations of wireless telegraphy down in the gulf-the Marconi system. We have investigated on the sound between New York and Boston a new invention which is called the submarine bell signal. Examinations have been made from time to time for over three years of this invention. It has been recommended specially by flie lighthouse board and all the shippping interests, but we have not yet adopted it.' The question may come up later in the supplementaries if we can come to some satisfactory arrangement with the inventors. Besides these wireless stations
I So
we are providing new7 fog alarms to replace those which have become obsolete.

What has the bon. gentleman done with regard to the pilots V Two, if not three of them were blamed entirely for certain accidents. I understand that the pilotage system on the St. Lawrence, has not been for years what it should be, and steps should be taken to make it perfect. No pilot should be allowed to take charge of a vessel unless he has a certificate.

The hou. gentleman must know that the pilots are obliged to submit to an examination every year and they cannot get a branch before they have served a certain number of years as apprentice-seven years, I think. It is well known that during the past few7 years the present government have been trying to improve the pilotage system. An investigation into the whole system was made in 1897, and the recommendations of the commissioners were embodied in laws adopted by parliament from time to time since that date. I certainly am not open to any reproach for any neglect in that respect. When I took charge of the department, I put myself in communication with the pilots, and I had special means of knowing the conditions as I had been a harbour commissioner in Montreal during many years. I convinced the pilots that they could improve their methods and inspire greater confidence by organizing differently, and I induced them to renounce their allegiance to the harbour commissioners of Montreal, and accept entirely the direction and control of the Department of Marine and Fisheries, under certain rules and regulations which were approved by them. Since the opening of navigation, there has only been one accident on the St. Lawrence route, which could be attributable to the fault of the pilots, and that is the extraordinary accident which occurred three weeks ago, when a steamer of the Richelieu Company, the ' Canada ' came into collision with the ' Cape Breton.' The investigation into this accident w7ill begin Monday, and the responsibility be placed where it belongs. There w7ere two accidents last year on the Saguenay river due to the fault of the pilots. A boat was stranded on the rocks in broad daylight, and this was not due to any lack of aids to navigation, but to the fault of the pilot, who did not know the Saguenay route.
What sort of an examination did he pass ?

I do not control the examinations to which these pilots are submitted by the Quebec Harbour Commissioners. This particular pilot had served seven years apprenticeship and had been a pilot for quite a number of years. Unfortunately, the harbour commissioners of Quebec did not provide pilots for the Sams VISED EDITION

guenay that knew the river as they should know it. I have now taken over control of the pilotage for the Saguenay river, and hope to he able to provide pilots that have passed a special examination for that river. The fact is, we have been working on these improvements for every quarter where they have been found necessary, and we have been doing our best to inspire the confidence of the shipping interest. The result is that any improvement that we have made is received -with nothing but praise by the shipping people.
Will the hon. minister explain the expenditure in connection with the lighting system in the harbour of Halifax 5

I take it that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Blain) refers to the lightship. A lightship had been contracted for my predecessor, to be delivered, I think, in August. The ship was delivered a little late, but still it was installed last fall. This lightship was called the Lurcher, and was installed on the Lurcher shoal, always a difficult-point and one for which this improvement has been asked for years and years. The installation of this lightship has given great satisfaction to the shipping interest.
I understand that there had also been the purchase of a wharf there ?

We purchased a wharf at Dartmouth on the other side of the harbour from Halifax. It was purchased from Mr. George J. Troop. We wanted the property as a place to keep the oil, gas buoys and other things of that kind necessary in connection with the appliances for the' safety of navigation in the waters of that section. We have not yet expended any rnopey on the property itself, but, in the supplementary estimates we shall ask a little money to put the property in such a condition as to make it useful to the department.

The hon. gentleman did not state the price.
Mr. *PREFONTAINE. I think it was $15,000. It was considered a very low price. The department was told that we could not get a property at that figure, but we managed to do it.
Have any of these gas lights been established in Georgian bay ? If not. how many is it contemplated to establish during the present year, and where are they to be ?
Eight gas and one gas beacon.
Where ?
On Kill Bear Point.
As I understand the minister's explanation this afternoon, the inten-
tion is to do away with the series of light keepers and establish acetylene gas lights.

That is the intention. But we can only make these improvements as we get the necessary appliances. In order to carry on the work extensively on Georgian bay, we shall require a station somewhere about Parry Sound I do not know exactly where we shall choose the site-to keep apparatus, to prepare the gas buoys and gas, and keep the holders and carry on the work of changing them.
I suppose the hon. gentleman has estimated the cost of maintenance of the acetylene system as against the old system.
I gave the figures the other night. They showed, I think, that the lights would be about thirty per cent cheaper and about five or six times more penetrating and with greater illuminating power.
What is the illuminant on the Lurcher lightship ?
Electricity.
She has a dynamo aboard?
Yes.

In reading the reports of the commissioner in charge of the investigations into casualties, I find it indicated that the pilots were not well posted at all. For instance, in the investigation into the wreck of the ' Iberian,' Captain Salmon the commissioner says :
The court is of the opinion that pilots should have a better knowledge of the compass and charts and steer by compass when the buoys are so far apart as to be invisible one from the other, instead of trusting entirely to shore marks, which in the present instance were ill-defined.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. E. D. Smith) surely will not hold-me responsible for pilots who were examined fifteen or twenty years ago. I am trying to improve the system as I have already had the honour to state. It is true that this is one of the points to which attention has been drawn by Captain Salmon, and we are toying to improve the examinations for pilots. For instance, this year the examination we have given the pilots to pass is most severe, so as to make sure that only those are appointed who are able to render the services we expect from them, and to inspire the confidence of the people. But surely I cannot be held responsible for pilots passed under insufficient examination by the harbour commissioners of Quebec or of Montreal or of Halifax. They were not under my control as those at Montreal and the Saguenay are at the present time. The others are not directly under my control and I cannot reach them except by amending the law. And surely hon. gen-

tlemen opposite will grant me the necessary time to have these laws passed. This year I have had a couple of amendments put through, and I have others to propose. But these things must be done gradually. You have to deal with a body of people who have been left, to a certain extent, independent and, of course, there is always a good deal of difficulty in reaching them, and it is impossible to reach them at once-it takes time. Formerly, for instance, candidates were not examined as regards their sight or hearing, and in other respects the examination was very poor. We have changed that as regards the pilots of Montreal and we are trying to do the same thing with regard to the rest of the Dominion wherever we can arrive at an improvement.

I would suggest that the authority seems to be very much divided. The Minister of Marine has under his care only a portion of the pilots. The harbour commissioners of Quebec seem to have control Of some of them. I think this parliament would be very glad to allow the minister opportunity to bring in amendments of the law so as to take under his care the whole of these pilots.

I suppose the lion gentleman will consult my hon. friend from Montmorency (Mr. Casgrain) in the matter because he is the defender of the pilots and will have to take care of them. I am going as. fast as I can, and some think I am going too fast, but I am doing the best 1 can.
In case the minister amends the Act, would he suggest that these old pilots, who were examined fifteen years ago, will have to pass a new examination 1

By all means.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: How many of these are new men last year ?

They change to some extent. Sometimes they think that they will improve their situation and they leave the department and we replace them by others, and do the best we can under the circumstances. I think there are four new ones.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
That is a heavy increase for one year.
To provide for wireless stations at Point Amour, Heath Point, Anticosti, Fame Point, Cape Race, Belle Isle and Sable island, $25,000.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Has this money been spent ?
No, part of it is being spent at the present time. I think that by the 15th of August the four stations will be installed.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: What is the total cost of one of these stations ?
About $5,000. We have to provide a boat with a crew to carry the material and workmen.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: $25,000 was voted last year. Was that spent ?

No, that was returned. The operation of the Fame Point station began bn June 9th. The test has proven that it is a complete success. Communication was maintained at a distance of 65 miles up and down with the ' Parisian.' It takes about fourteen days to establish a station, and the work is now going on. The contract made with the Marconi Company is that if it is a success they are to be paid, if it is not we pay nothing except the expenditure which we incur in carrying material and men to the different stations.
How many stations are there now ?

We have only one estabiished at the present time, but the contract is for four stations. However, we intend to establish more. We intend to establish a station on Sable island, one at Sydney, one at Fame Point, one at Cape Race and one at Belle Isle.
Are most of the ocean liners coming into Montreal fitted with wireless telegraphy apparatus, so that they can communicate with these stations ?
Three of the lines, the Allan Line, the Elder-Dempster Line and the Beaver Line are fitted with the apparatus, the other lines are coming in and installing the apparatus.
Does the minister intend to establish a station at each of these points ?
Yes.
There are seven stations then, not four.
We have contracted only for four, but we intend to establish more.
Then I am correct in understanding that $25,000 is sufficient to provide for the seven stations ?

No, not for the seven. I do not think we will have time to establish that number before the vote lapses. We will have to provide in the supplementary estimates for a further sum, deducting whatever has not been expended out of this sum.
To provide for the expenses of the Montreal Pilot Commissioner's Court, $2,000.
How many cases were tried by this court last year ?
I think there have been two or three cases tried by this commissioner.
What is the nature of the cases ?
$18,000 was expended last year for investigations which took place through this commissioner in Montreal.

Would the minister state the number of casualties and wrecks that took place in Canadian waters ? The report gives the details of those that occurred in the Gulf of St. Lawrence only, and simply gives the total number of those that occurred in Canadian waters. Where can one ascertain the particulars of those wrecks that occurred in Canadian waters, but not in the Gulf of St. Lawrence V
Every wreck that was investigated is mentioned in the report.
but those that take place outside of Canadian waters are not investigated.
I am speaking of those that did occur in Canadian waters, but not in the Gulf of St. Lawrence or the St. Law-renpe river.
On pages 86 to 93 of the report of the department the hon. gentleman will find a complete report of the investigations into wrecks.
Those investigations, I take it, refer to those casualties that occurred in the Gulf of iSt. Lawrence and from that out.
Every place where there is a casualty.
This refers to the investigations that were held ; was an investigation held into every wreck that occurred ?

An investigation was held into every wreck where we had jurisdiction. That was the demand made by the different boards of trade throughout the country.
Repairs to wharfs, $3,000.	'
Where are these wharfs located 5

Small sums - are spent by the department in repairing wharfs situated in different parts of the country which are under the control of the department not exceeding $15.
Scientific institutions and hydrographic surveys, magnetic observatory, $2,700.
Where is that 1

At Agincourt, near Toronto.
Hydrographic surveys, $35,000.
Is the hydrographic survey being continued on Lake Superior 1
Yes.
How long do you expect it will take the department to complete the work up there ?

It is pretty hard for me to say. I am taking over the hydrographic survey work of the Department of Railways and Canals and Department of Public Works. I am organizing these surveys in such a way as to be in a position within the next five or six months to know exactly how long it will take to complete what has been undertaken. There is work that has been done for the last five years on certain rivers and lakes but the charts have not been published. This is a service that will have to be completely organized. I suppose the work in the Lake Superior region will be completed in a year fro in now. I do not say that the charts will be completed but
1

we will be able to have them published as soon as their preparation is completed. We have been asked to survey large lakes in different parts of the country. Of. course we will do that gradually as the expansion of the country goes on. We will take the Ottawa river this year because a hydrographic survey of the Ottawa river has never been properly made. The navigators] on the Ottawa river are very anxious to get a chart of that river.
Mr. SPROtTLE. Where were you operating last year ?
On Lake Superior. Mr. SPROtTLE. Lake Superior is a large lake.

Near Port Arthur.
Mr. SPROtTLE. Do you intend to start another party to survey the St. Lawrence and allow the work to go on on Lake Superior as you have been doing for some years past ?

Oh, of course.
Marine hospitals-care of sick seamen in the marine hospitals in the maritime provinces and repairs to marine hospitals, $50,000.
Mr. SPROtTLE. Are these confined to the maritime provinces ?

No, in other places we make arrangements with the local hospitals by ..which seamen are taken care of at a certain price.
Mr. SPROtTLE. You pay so much per capita ?
Yes.

What is the expense entailed for attending sick' mariners in the harbour of St. John and how are they attended ? I notice that the department have collected in sick mariner's dues over $6,000 at that port andJ I would like to know how ffiuch was expended in looking after the sick mariners ?

' There was collected at St. John, $6,466 and in the province of New Brunswick 428 s'ick seamen were treated. I have not the figures showing how much it cost. If they are treated at the hospital they are charged at ninety cents per day. We collect a good deal more1 than we pay and that is a very live question. It was brought up last year but there was no decision arrived at. Surely we will have to come to some understanding with the shipping people so that they may take care of their own seamen as is done in other countries. It is my opinion that they should, although I do not know whether that opinion will be endorsed by the government.

I would like to ask the hon. minister whether the amount paid to
the hospital for each sick sailor per day has been increased from ninety cents per day .
We are going to put 'it at the same rate as in Montreal, where it is $1.20 per day.
When will that increase, commence 'i

On the 1st July.
Steamboat inspection-inspector of Dominion steamers and fog-alarms, $1,700.
I would like to ask the hon. minister how long this gentleman has been in this position as inspector of Dominion steamers and fog alarms ?
About twenty years.

It would seem from the report of the investigations into the shipwrecks that he has not been looking very carefully after the requirements of the route. With regard to the stranding of the barque ' Sardhana ' the report states with reference to the aids to navigation :
The fog system at Pointe des Monts is insufficient ; the evidence of various witnesses goes to show that it was impossible to bear the fog signal even after the vessel stranded.

It is on the rec-commendation of Mr. Stephens and the chief engineer that we have decided to incur this heavy expenditure to improve the fog alarms. The old machinery was good, but it was not strong enough, and as the changing involved a large expenditure, and as other things were more pressing, the department did not go on with the expenditure but we have decided to do so now.
The%iinister cannot spend money on any service in the Dominion where it is more needed.
Give me a chance ; I am well disposed.

The department is spending a great deal more money now than formerly, and I regret that there has not been a corresponding increase in the efficiency of the service. I would urge on the minister to devote all his energies to perfecting the route and making it as safe as possible.

Yon may be sure I will.
